Fixed monthly payment::The EMI stays level while the interest and principal parts shift each month.
Reducing balance::Interest is charged only on the outstanding balance, not the original loan.
Zero rate supported::A 0 percent rate splits the principal evenly across all months.

page.mistakes:
Using the annual rate directly::The formula needs the monthly rate, which is the annual rate divided by 1200.
Expecting the final instalment to match::Rounding in real contracts can make the last payment slightly different.
Ignoring fees and insurance::The estimate covers principal and interest only, not processing charges.
page.limits:
The schedule preview shows six months, not the full term.
Tenure is capped at 600 months and must be a whole number.
Displayed figures are rounded to two decimals and exclude fees, tax and insurance.
page.faqs:
How is EMI calculated?::EMI is P times r times (1 + r) to the power n, divided by (1 + r) to the power n minus 1. P is the loan principal, r is the monthly decimal rate and n is the number of months. A zero rate is handled by dividing the principal evenly across the full term.
Why does my EMI stay the same each month?::The formula solves for a payment that clears the balance exactly by the end of the term. Each month the interest portion is calculated on the remaining balance, so it falls over time. The principal portion rises by the same amount, keeping the total payment level from the first month to the last.
What is total interest?::Total interest is the EMI multiplied by the number of months, minus the amount you borrowed. It is the full cost of borrowing under a reducing balance schedule. A longer term lowers the monthly payment but usually raises total interest because the balance stays outstanding for more months.
Why might my bank bill differ?::Lenders usually round the EMI to whole currency units and then adjust the final instalment so the balance clears exactly. They may also add processing fees, insurance or tax, which this estimate does not include. Small differences in the rate used for calculation can change the result as well.
page.trustBody: Uses the standard reducing balance EMI formula with a six month preview. Updated 26 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a BMI Calculator?
page.whatIs:
Body mass index, or BMI, is a weight to height ratio used as a quick screening measure for adults. In metric units the formula is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. In imperial units it is weight in pounds divided by height in inches squared, then multiplied by the conversion factor 703. A BMI of 22.9 can come from 70 kilograms at a height of 1.75 metres.

The World Health Organization groups adult results into four bands. Below 18.5 is underweight, 18.5 up to 25 is healthy, 25 up to 30 is overweight, and 30 or above is obese. These are population level cutoffs, not a diagnosis for any one person. This tool also works out the weight span that would put your height inside the healthy band, using 18.5 and 25 as the boundaries, so you can see the numbers behind the guidance.

BMI has clear limits. It cannot tell muscle from fat, so athletes and people with high muscle mass may be classed as overweight despite low body fat. It is not validated for children, teenagers or pregnancy, where age based percentiles or other clinical measures are used. Body fat distribution and other risk factors also matter. Treat the result as a starting point for a conversation with a health professional, not as medical advice. All calculation happens in your browser and your numbers are not uploaded.

Formula shown::Each result includes the arithmetic so you can check the number yourself.
Private by design::All math runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
page.mistakes:
Using the wrong unit::Switch the unit control before typing, because kilograms and pounds need different formulas.
Entering height in feet::Imperial height is taken in inches, so convert feet and inches to a single inch value first.
Treating BMI as a diagnosis::The category is a screening band, not a medical verdict about body fat or health.
Ignoring the range::A single BMI value hides how much weight change would move you into another band.
page.limits:

Athletes and very muscular people may be misclassified.
Children, teenagers and pregnant people need different measures.
The healthy range uses BMI 18.5 to 25 as boundaries and is rounded to one decimal.
page.faqs:
How is BMI calculated?::In metric units, divide weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. In imperial units, divide weight in pounds by height in inches squared and multiply by 703. The calculator shows the exact formula it used under the result, so you can check the number without trusting a black box.
What does my BMI category mean?::The category places your number into a standard adult band. Below 18.5 is underweight, 18.5 to 25 is healthy, 25 to 30 is overweight, and 30 or more is obese. These bands describe populations and do not diagnose an individual, so discuss concerns with a health professional.
Why is the healthy weight range a span?::A height can support many healthy weights because BMI is a ratio. The tool works out the weight at BMI 18.5 and at BMI 25 for your height, then shows that span in your chosen unit. It is a guide, not a target, and individual needs vary.
Does BMI measure body fat?::No. BMI uses only weight and height, so it cannot separate muscle, bone and fat. A muscular person may have a high BMI with low body fat, while an older adult may have a healthy BMI with high body fat. Other measures are needed for a fuller picture.
Can I use this for a child?::No. BMI cutoffs here are for adults. Children and teenagers need age and sex based percentile charts, because body composition changes during growth. Pregnancy also needs different guidance. For anyone in those groups, ask a clinician which measure is appropriate.
page.trustBody: Applies metric and imperial BMI formulas with WHO adult cutoffs and a healthy weight span. Reviewed 26 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Pomodoro Timer?
page.whatIs:
A Pomodoro Timer is a simple clock for timeboxing: it alternates a fixed work interval with a short rest, then inserts a longer rest after a set of rounds. The method takes its name from the Italian word for tomato, used for the kitchen timer that Francesco Cirillo reportedly used in the late 1980s. The common pattern is 25 minutes of focus, five minutes of rest and a 15 minute break after four rounds. A completed work interval is often called a Pomodoro.

The point of the method is not the numbers. A fixed block makes a large task approachable, and the break is a real stopping point rather than a vague pause. Keeping the same lengths across a session also makes it easier to estimate how many blocks a piece of work needs.

This tool puts those three lengths in the input pane as inline minute steppers. Press Start to run the countdown, Pause to freeze it, and Reset to return to the first round. A work round adds one to the round counter and moves to a short break. Every fourth work round moves to the long break instead. A short written notice marks each change of phase.

Everything happens in this browser tab. The timer uses a one second interval that is cleaned up when the tool unmounts, plays no sound, asks for no permission and sends no data anywhere.
page.howToTitle: How to use Pomodoro Timer
page.howTo:
Set the work, short break and long break lengths with the inline steppers.
Press Start to begin the focus countdown.
Press Pause if you need to stop, then Start again to resume from the same second.
Watch the round counter rise when a work session ends and a break begins.
Use Reset to return to the first round and the full work duration.
page.useCases:
Study sessions::Keep a 25 minute focus block before a five minute break.
Writing work::Finish one section of a draft before the countdown ends.
Code reviews::Give each review a fixed block so the queue keeps moving.
Team breaks::Let a group take the same short break after four rounds.
page.mistakes:
Skipping the short break::The break is part of the method, not an optional extra between rounds.
Changing a length mid round::Edits apply to the next phase, so the current countdown keeps its original length.
Expecting an alert sound::This timer shows a written notice in the tool bar and plays no audio.
page.limits:
Durations accept whole minutes from 1 to 180.
The long break arrives after every fourth completed work round.
Timer state is held in this tab and is lost when you close or reload the page.
page.faqs:
What are the standard Pomodoro lengths?::The usual pattern is 25 minutes of focus, a five minute short break after each round, and a 15 minute long break after four rounds. Those values are loaded as the sample. You can change any of them, but the four-round long break rule stays fixed.
Does the timer make a sound?::No. This tool never plays audio and never asks for microphone or notification permission. When a phase ends you get a short written notice in the tool bar, and the next phase starts with its own countdown and label.
What happens when I pause?::Pause freezes the remaining seconds where they are. Press Start again and the countdown continues from that point rather than starting over. Reset returns the phase to focus, clears the round counter and restores the full work duration.
Why is the long break shown as four rounds away?::The counter tracks completed work rounds toward the long break. After a long break the count continues with the next group of four, so the number shown is always the remaining rounds in the current group.
Is my progress saved?::No. Everything lives in this browser tab and nothing is sent to a server. Closing or reloading the page clears the countdown and the round count, so treat the timer as a session tool rather than a long term log.
page.trustBody: Runs the full focus and break cycle locally with a one second interval that is cleaned up on unmount. No audio, no network and no saved history. Updated 26 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Coffee Calories Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A coffee calories calculator estimates the energy in a cup by adding the calories of every part of the drink. This tool starts with a coffee portion for the chosen base and size, adds a size-scaled milk serving, includes chocolate for a mocha, then adds syrup pumps, sugar teaspoons and one dollop of whipped cream.

The arithmetic is deliberately simple. Espresso, latte, cappuccino and mocha portions come from shot counts that grow with the cup size, while brewed and cold brew use typical volumes. Milk is counted at roughly 180 ml per serving: small drinks use a fraction of a serving and large drinks use up to two. Whole milk is about 110 kcal per serving, skim 65, oat 80 and almond 30, so changing the milk changes both energy and macros without hiding a second milk allowance in the base.

Each syrup pump contributes 20 kcal and 5 g of carbohydrate, and each teaspoon of sugar adds 16 kcal and 4 g of carbohydrate. Whipped cream is one standard dollop at 60 kcal, 1 g protein, 1 g carbohydrate and 6 g fat. Protein and carbohydrate provide 4 kcal per gram while fat provides 9, which is how the macro bars work out their shares of macro energy. Values are rounded only for display, so the copyable breakdown keeps the full arithmetic.

Cafe recipes vary widely. A chain latte may use a larger shot, a flavoured syrup or a different milk volume, so treat the result as a planning estimate rather than a label. If you have a nutrition label for a specific product, use the custom food entry in a meal calculator instead. Everything here runs in your browser and no drink details are stored.

Milk: Oat milk
Syrup pumps: 1

Six drink bases::Espresso, brewed coffee, cold brew, latte, cappuccino and mocha each start from a coffee portion.
Three cup sizes::Small, medium and large scale the coffee portion and the milk servings together.
Four milk choices::Whole, skim, oat and almond milk use typical values for one 180 ml serving.
Simple additions::Syrup pumps, sugar teaspoons and one dollop of cream have fixed energy values.
Live macro bars::Protein, carbs and fat update instantly and show their share of macro energy.

Counting milk twice::Pick the milk once. The base is only the coffee portion, so the milk you choose is the only milk counted.
Treating pumps as free::One syrup pump adds about 20 kcal and 5 g of carbohydrate, so several pumps add up quickly.
Assuming cafe accuracy::Recipes, cup sizes and milk volumes vary, so read this as an estimate rather than a label.

page.faqs:
How are coffee calories calculated?::The tool adds the coffee portion for your base and cup size, a size scaled milk serving, chocolate for a mocha, then syrup, sugar and cream. Protein and carbohydrate count 4 kcal per gram and fat counts 9, and the total is rounded only when it is displayed.
Does the milk choice replace anything?::No. Each base describes the coffee and flavouring portion only, so the milk option always adds the drink's milk. Choose no milk for a black drink, or pick oat or almond to see how a swap changes both the energy and the macro bars.
What does one syrup pump add?::One pump adds 20 kcal and 5 g of carbohydrate with no protein or fat. You can set between 0 and 10 pumps. A teaspoon of sugar is a separate addition at 16 kcal and 4 g of carbohydrate, so the two steppers are counted independently.
Are these numbers exact?::No. They use typical serving sizes and rounded nutrition values, while real cafes vary their shot counts, milk volumes and recipes. Use the result to compare options and plan your day, and follow a printed label when you need a precise figure for a packaged product.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Drink values use standard serving estimates and macro energy factors of 4, 4 and 9. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to Read Your Coffee Calorie Breakdown
page.guidance:
The coffee calculator adds energy from the base, milk, chocolate, syrup, sugar and cream, then splits it into protein, carbs and fat. Treat the total as a planning figure built from standard servings. The "Where the calories come from" bars show which part drives the number, since milk often outweighs the coffee in a latte and a mocha adds chocolate on top. Protein and carbohydrate count 4 kcal per gram, fat counts 9, and that is how each macro bar takes its share.

Suppose you build a medium oat milk latte with one syrup pump, one teaspoon of sugar and whipped cream. The result is about 226 kcal, with roughly 120 from milk and 60 from cream. Dropping the cream saves 60 kcal, and swapping oat for almond milk can cut the milk share from about 120 to 45 kcal because almond milk is roughly 30 kcal per 180 ml serving against oat milk's 80. Use those swaps to compare orders before you buy, and follow a printed label for a bottled coffee when you need an exact figure.

page.whatIs:
A meal calories and macros calculator adds the energy from each food you eat and separates that energy into protein, carbohydrate and fat. This tool keeps a small table of everyday foods with one serving each. You search or quick add a food, change the number of servings, and read the new total immediately.

The arithmetic is a sum of products. For every food, the tool multiplies its calories, protein, carbs and fat by the number of servings, then adds the columns across the whole meal. A food with 165 kcal and two servings contributes 330 kcal. The same rule applies to a custom item you enter from a package label, so nothing is estimated twice.

Macro bars show the share of energy from each macronutrient rather than a share of plate weight. Protein and carbohydrate supply about 4 kcal per gram, while fat supplies about 9 kcal per gram. Those factors turn grams into energy, and the bar width is that energy divided by the energy from all three macros. A food with almost no carbohydrate will therefore show a small carb bar even if its gram figure looks similar to another macro.

The bundled table uses common household servings such as one apple, one cup of cooked rice or 100 g of cooked chicken. Real portions and brands vary, and cooking methods change the weight of foods like pasta and rice. Treat the result as a planning estimate, not a medical figure. All work happens in your browser, and clearing the meal removes everything from view.
page.howToTitle: How to use Meal Calories & Macros Calculator
page.howTo:
Search for a food or pick one of the quick add buttons.
Set the number of servings with the stepper beside each food.
Enter a custom item when your food is not in the table.
Read the total calories and the macro bars in the result pane.
Copy the summary or clear the meal to start again.

White rice (1 cup): 1 serving

page.exampleOutput:
Chicken breast (100 g) x 1: 165 kcal
White rice (1 cup) x 1: 206 kcal
Broccoli (1 cup) x 1: 55 kcal
Total: 426 kcal
Protein: 39.0 g
Carbs: 56.0 g
Fat: 4.6 g
page.exampleNote: Each row uses one serving from the bundled table, and the totals are the sum of all three rows.
page.mistakes:
Using raw weights for cooked values::The table lists a named serving, so weigh the food in the state described by that serving.
Forgetting the quantity::Each stepper counts servings, so two portions double the calories and every macro.
Assuming every brand matches::Packaged foods vary, so use the printed label for a custom item when you have one.
page.limits:
The bundled table holds a small set of common everyday foods.
Servings run from 0 to 99 in steps of half a serving.
Custom values are capped at 5000 kcal and 500 g per macro to keep the summary readable.
page.faqs:
Where do the food values come from?::The tool bundles a small table of everyday foods with a typical serving for each one, such as one medium banana or 100 g of cooked chicken. These are rounded reference values, not laboratory measurements, and a real product can differ. When you have a package label, enter its numbers as a custom item instead.
How do the serving steppers work?::Every food you add gets its own stepper, starting at one serving. Each click raises or lowers the count by half a serving, and you can also type a value directly. The tool multiplies that food's calories and macros by the count, then adds the result to the meal totals instantly.
Can I add a food that is not in the table?::Yes. Enter a name plus the calories, protein, carbs and fat for one serving, then press Add custom item. The values are checked before they join the meal, and you can remove the item later. Nothing you type is uploaded or remembered between visits.
Why do the macro bars differ from the calorie total?::The bars show each macro's share of the energy supplied by protein, carbs and fat, using 4, 4 and 9 kcal per gram. The calorie total uses the food values from the table or label, which may include small rounding differences. That is why a bar is a share of macro energy, not a direct percentage of the label calories.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Food values are typical servings and the macro bars use 4, 4 and 9 kcal per gram. Updated 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How Servings Change Your Meal Calorie Total
page.guidance:
Meal Calories and Macros Calculator sums each food by multiplying its calories, protein, carbs and fat by the servings you set, then adds the columns across the meal. Read the total as the sum of those rows, and use the macro bars to see how much of the energy comes from protein, carbs and fat. Because the bars use 4, 4 and 9 kcal per gram, a food low in carbohydrate shows a thin carb bar even when its gram figure looks similar to another macro.

Add chicken breast, one cup of white rice and one cup of broccoli at one serving each. The tool reports about 426 kcal in total, with 39 g protein, 56 g carbs and 4.6 g fat. Raising the rice to two servings adds another 206 kcal and roughly doubles its carbohydrate contribution, which is the fastest way to see how a portion change moves the numbers. When a packaged food is not in the table, enter its label values for one serving as a custom item so nothing gets counted twice.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Daily Water Intake Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A daily water intake calculator turns body weight and activity into a practical fluid target for the day. Our tool starts from a simple rule: about 35 millilitres of fluid per kilogram of body weight. That baseline covers ordinary daily losses through breathing, skin and urine for a healthy adult. The calculator then multiplies the baseline by an activity factor and adds optional boosts before converting the total into glasses and bottles.

If you enter pounds, the tool first converts to kilograms using 0.45359237 kilograms per pound. The activity factors are 1.0 for sedentary, 1.1 for light, 1.2 for moderate and 1.35 for active. For a 70 kilogram adult with a moderate activity level, the baseline is 2450 ml and the activity adjusted figure is 2940 ml. Selecting the exercise boost adds 500 ml, and the hot climate boost adds another 500 ml.

The glass and bottle breakdown uses a 250 ml glass and a 500 ml bottle, rounded up so you always reach the target. For the 2940 ml example, that is 12 glasses or 6 bottles. Totals are rounded to the nearest 10 ml so the numbers stay readable.

These figures are starting points, not prescriptions. Fluid needs change with body size, training load, altitude, humidity, illness and medication. Pregnancy and some medical conditions raise or lower requirements, and thirst is a useful signal for many people. This calculator assumes a healthy adult and does not account for sodium loss, kidney conditions or fluid obtained from food, which can supply a meaningful share of daily intake.
page.howToTitle: How to use Daily Water Intake Calculator
page.howTo:

Pick the activity level that matches a typical day.
Turn on the exercise or hot climate boost if either applies.
Read the daily target, then use the glass and bottle counts to pace your drinking.
Copy the result to keep the figures.
page.features:
Weight based baseline::Uses 35 ml per kilogram after converting pounds when needed.
Activity factors::Scales the baseline from 1.0 for sedentary up to 1.35 for active.
Optional boosts::Adds 500 ml for exercise and 500 ml for a hot climate.
Glass and bottle view::Splits the target into 250 ml glasses and 500 ml bottles, rounded up.
page.mistakes:
Using a target weight::Enter your current weight, not a weight you are aiming for.
Double counting fluid from food::Food contributes water, so treat the target as a guide rather than an exact requirement.
Ignoring climate and training::A hot day or a long session can raise needs well above the baseline.
page.limits:
Baseline assumes a healthy adult with no medical fluid restriction.
Weights outside 1 to 400 kg or 2 to 900 lb are rejected.
Boosts are fixed amounts and are not tailored to session length.
page.faqs:
How is the daily target calculated?::The tool multiplies your weight in kilograms by 35 ml, scales that baseline by an activity factor, then adds 500 ml for exercise and 500 ml for a hot climate when selected. The total is rounded to the nearest 10 ml and split into glasses and bottles.
Does the calculator handle pounds?::Yes. Choose pounds in the unit switch and enter your weight as usual. The tool converts it to kilograms with a factor of 0.45359237 before applying the formula, then reports the result in millilitres with glass and bottle counts.
Why are glasses and bottles rounded up?::A 250 ml glass and a 500 ml bottle are whole servings, so the counts round up to make sure you reach or pass the target. For 2940 ml you would need 12 glasses or 6 bottles. Copy the report to see each figure.
Is this medical advice?::No. The estimate is a general guide for healthy adults and does not replace advice from a clinician. Illness, medication, pregnancy, kidney conditions and heavy training can all change fluid needs, so ask a professional if you have concerns.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Weight, activity and boost choices are processed entirely in your browser, and only your preferred unit is remembered. Last updated 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to Read Your Daily Water Target
page.guidance:
Daily Water Intake Calculator starts from about 35 ml of fluid per kilogram of body weight, then scales that baseline by an activity factor and adds any exercise or hot climate boost. The total is a general target in millilitres, which the tool converts into rounded up glasses of 250 ml or bottles of 500 ml. Read the base, after activity and extra boost rows to see what moved the number, and use the glass and bottle counts simply as a way to pace your drinking across the day.

For a 70 kg adult with moderate activity and no boosts, the baseline is 2450 ml and the activity adjusted target is 2940 ml, which the tool shows as 12 glasses or 6 bottles. Turn on the exercise boost and the target becomes 3440 ml, about 14 glasses, because each boost adds a fixed 500 ml. Use the switches to compare a normal day with a training day, and rely on thirst alongside the number since illness, medication and conditions such as kidney disease can shift real needs.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Sleep Cycle Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A sleep cycle calculator uses the roughly 90 minute length of a full sleep cycle to suggest wake times or bedtimes that avoid waking in deep sleep. Our tool works in both directions. Give it a bedtime and it lists wake times; give it a wake time and it lists bedtimes.

The arithmetic is simple. Each option adds the fall-asleep buffer to a whole number of 90 minute cycles. For bedtime mode, wake time equals bedtime plus buffer plus cycles times 90 minutes. For wake mode, bedtime equals wake time minus buffer minus cycles times 90 minutes. Results wrap around the 24 hour clock, so an early morning time is shown correctly. The tool lists three to seven cycles and marks five cycles as the recommended option, which is just under eight hours in bed including the buffer.

A 15 minute default buffer is used because most people do not fall asleep the moment their head touches the pillow. You can change it from 0 to 60 minutes in five minute steps. With a 23:00 bedtime, a 15 minute buffer and five cycles, the suggested wake time is 06:45. With a 07:00 wake time, the matching bedtime is 23:15.

The model assumes a regular 90 minute cycle and ignores individual variation, sleep debt and naps. It does not track sleep stages or measure how well you slept. Treat the times as a starting point for a consistent schedule rather than a precise biological prediction.

page.mistakes:
Ignoring the buffer::Falling asleep takes time, so the first cycle starts after the buffer you set.
Assuming fixed stages::Sleep cycles vary in length, so these times are a guide and not a measurement.
Forgetting midnight wrap::Early morning times belong to the next day, which the list handles automatically.
page.limits:
Cycle length is fixed at 90 minutes.
The buffer is limited to 0 to 60 minutes in five minute steps.
Only three to seven cycles are listed.
page.faqs:
How does the calculator choose the times?::It adds a fall-asleep buffer to whole 90 minute cycles. In bedtime mode it adds that total to your bedtime; in wake mode it subtracts it from your wake time. Results wrap past midnight, and the five cycle option is highlighted as a common target.
Why is five cycles highlighted?::Five 90 minute cycles are often cited as a balanced night of sleep. With the default 15 minute buffer that is seven hours and 45 minutes in bed. It is a suggestion, not a rule, so compare the other rows and choose the one that fits your schedule.
Can I use a 12 hour clock?::The time field uses a 24 hour value such as 23:00 or 07:00. The displayed list follows your locale format, which may show AM and PM. You can change the buffer in five minute steps from 0 to 60 minutes.
Does this track my sleep stages?::No. It only schedules clock times from a fixed 90 minute cycle length. It cannot measure when you actually fall asleep or which stage you are in, and it does not replace a sleep diary or advice from a clinician.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. All scheduling happens locally in your browser, and only your preferred mode and buffer are remembered. Last updated 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to Pick a Wake Time From Bedtime
page.guidance:
Sleep Cycle Calculator uses the roughly 90 minute length of a full sleep cycle to suggest times that avoid waking in deep sleep. In bedtime mode it adds your fall asleep buffer plus whole cycles to the time you enter, while wake mode runs the arithmetic backwards to suggest bedtimes. The highlighted five cycle option is just under eight hours in bed including the buffer, and times past midnight wrap to the next day. Treat the list as a scheduling guide, not a measurement of your sleep stages.

With a 23:00 bedtime and the default 15 minute buffer, five cycles puts your wake time at 06:45, while four cycles gives 05:15 and six gives 08:15. If you must wake at 07:00, switch modes and the matching bedtime appears as 23:15. Adjust the buffer in five minute steps when you know you take longer to fall asleep, and compare the neighbouring rows to pick a schedule that fits a fixed alarm. Use the result to build a consistent routine rather than expecting it to track how well you actually slept.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a TDEE Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A TDEE calculator estimates total daily energy expenditure, the number of calories your body uses in one day. It starts from basal metabolic rate, or BMR, which is the energy needed for basic functions at rest. The Mifflin-St Jeor equation is the standard starting point: multiply weight in kilograms by 10, add 6.25 times height in centimetres, subtract 5 times age in years, then add 5 for male or subtract 161 for female.

Basal rate alone ignores movement, so the tool multiplies it by an activity factor. The five factors are 1.2 for a sedentary week, 1.375 for light activity, 1.55 for moderate activity, 1.725 for active weeks and 1.9 for very active weeks or hard physical work. The product is your estimated daily burn. Maintenance is shown as the same number. The cut and gain rows shift it down or up by 500 kcal a day, which is a simple reference gap rather than a personal plan.

The result is an estimate from population equations, not a measurement. Illness, medication, sleep, body composition, pregnancy and training history all move real energy needs. Use the number as a starting point, then track body weight and intake over several weeks and adjust. For medical concerns, ask a clinician or registered dietitian. All arithmetic runs in your browser, and your entries are never uploaded.

page.features:
Mifflin-St Jeor::Basal rate uses 10 times kilograms plus 6.25 times centimetres minus 5 times age and a sex adjustment.
Five activity levels::Multipliers run from 1.2 for a sedentary week to 1.9 for very active days.
Reference rows::Maintenance, cut and gain sit around the daily total with a 500 kcal gap.
Formula shown::Each result prints the substituted arithmetic so you can check it.
Private by design::Everything runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
page.mistakes:
Using imperial units::This tool expects centimetres and kilograms, so convert pounds and inches first.
Picking a busy week::Choose a typical activity level rather than your most training-heavy week.
Reading the cut as advice::A 500 kcal gap is a reference point, not a personal prescription.
Ignoring the limits::Illness, medication and body composition all shift real energy needs.
page.limits:
Results are estimates for adults aged 16 and over.
The tool accepts 120 to 220 cm and 30 to 300 kg.
It cannot account for medical conditions or pregnancy.
Cut and gain values use a fixed 500 kcal a day gap.
page.faqs:
What formula does this TDEE calculator use?::It uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, which estimates basal metabolic rate from weight in kilograms, height in centimetres and age, with a fixed adjustment for sex. The daily total is that basal rate multiplied by your activity factor. The exact arithmetic appears under your result.
What do the cut and gain numbers mean?::Maintenance matches the daily total. The cut row subtracts 500 kcal a day and the gain row adds 500 kcal a day. They are simple reference points, not personal recommendations, and real progress depends on tracking intake and weight over several weeks.
Which activity level should I choose?::Pick the level that describes an ordinary week, not a single hard day. Sedentary means little exercise, light means one to three sessions, moderate means three to five, active means six or seven, and very active covers hard physical work or twice daily training.
How accurate is a TDEE calculator?::It is an estimate based on population equations, not a measurement. Illness, medication, sleep, body composition and genetics all move real energy needs. Use it as a starting point, then adjust with a food and weight log and ask a clinician for personal advice.
page.trustBody: Applies the adult Mifflin-St Jeor equation with five activity factors and a fixed 500 kcal reference gap. Reviewed 26 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to Read Your Daily Calorie Burn
page.guidance:
TDEE Calculator estimates your total daily energy expenditure by computing basal metabolic rate with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, then multiplying it by an activity factor. Basal rate covers basic functions at rest and the multiplier adds the movement of a typical week. The result in kcal per day is your maintenance figure, with cut and gain rows sitting 500 kcal below and above it as reference points. Read the printed formula to see which weight, height, age and sex adjustment produced the number.

Pick the activity level that describes an ordinary week rather than a busy training block, because the multipliers run from 1.2 for sedentary up to 1.9 for very active days. For example, a 30 year old male at 175 cm and 70 kg with moderate activity lands near 2560 kcal a day, and the cut row sits at about 2060 kcal. Use the figure as a starting point, then track weight and intake over several weeks and adjust. Illness, medication, sleep and body composition all shift real needs, so ask a clinician for personal advice.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Protein Target Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A protein target calculator converts a body weight into a daily number of grams of protein. It works in grams per kilogram of body weight, because needs scale with the amount of lean tissue you carry. You choose a goal and an activity level, and the tool returns a range plus a midpoint target you can copy.

The goal sets the base range. Maintenance uses 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram, muscle gain uses 1.6 to 2.2, and fat loss preservation uses 1.6 to 2.4. The higher end during a calorie deficit reflects the value of protein when you want to keep lean mass while total energy falls. Activity then shifts both ends slightly: low adds nothing, moderate adds 0.1 grams per kilogram and high adds 0.2. Your weight multiplies that range into grams per day, and the headline target is the midpoint rounded to whole grams.

These figures are general guidance drawn from sports nutrition position statements, not a clinical prescription. Requirements vary with age, training history, energy intake and health status. People with kidney disease or other medical conditions need individual advice, and pregnancy changes protein needs. Spread intake across meals rather than loading it into one sitting. All calculation happens in the browser, so your weight is never sent anywhere.
page.howToTitle: How to use Protein Target Calculator
page.howTo:
Enter your weight in kilograms.
Choose your goal.
Choose an activity level.
Read the daily target and range.
Copy the report.
page.features:
Goal ranges::Maintenance starts at 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg, muscle gain at 1.6 to 2.2, and fat loss preservation at 1.6 to 2.4.
Activity shift::Low adds nothing, moderate adds 0.1 g/kg and high adds 0.2 g/kg to both ends.
Daily conversion::The per kilogram range is multiplied by your weight to give grams per day.
Midpoint target::The headline target is the middle of the daily range rounded to whole grams.
Private by design::Your weight stays in the browser and is never uploaded.
page.mistakes:
Using pounds::The tool expects kilograms, so convert pounds by dividing by 2.2046 first.
Chasing the top end::The upper end is a range boundary, not a target you must hit every day.
Ignoring total diet::Protein targets sit inside an overall eating plan, not on top of unlimited calories.
Medical needs::Kidney disease and other conditions change safe protein intakes.
page.limits:
Accepts weights from 30 to 300 kilograms.
Ranges are general guidance for adults.
Activity shifts are fixed at 0, 0.1 or 0.2 g/kg.
The tool does not diagnose deficiencies or medical conditions.
page.faqs:
How much protein do I need per kilogram?::It depends on your goal. Common ranges are 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram for maintenance, 1.6 to 2.2 for muscle gain and 1.6 to 2.4 during fat loss when you want to preserve lean mass. Activity nudges those ranges slightly, and the tool shows both ends.
Why is there a range instead of one number?::Research gives ranges rather than a single value because people respond differently. The lower end suits lighter activity or steady weight, while the upper end gives more room during hard training or a calorie deficit. Your target here is the midpoint, and you can aim anywhere inside the range.
Does activity change the protein target?::Yes, modestly. This tool adds 0.1 grams per kilogram at moderate activity and 0.2 at high activity, with no addition at low activity. The shift applies to both ends of the goal range, so the daily gram range moves up as training load rises.
Is more protein always better?::No. Above a certain intake, extra protein is used for energy or converted rather than building more muscle. Very high intakes can displace other foods and may be unsuitable with kidney disease. Spread protein across meals and focus on total diet quality.
page.trustBody: Uses goal-based grams per kilogram ranges with a small activity adjustment and a midpoint target. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to read your protein target range
page.guidance:
The Protein Target Calculator gives a daily range in grams plus a midpoint target you can copy. The range is built from grams per kilogram of body weight, so your weight sets the scale of the result. The headline target is the midpoint of that range, rounded to whole grams. Read the low end as a workable minimum on lighter days and the high end as the top of the sports nutrition range for your goal. Aiming anywhere between the two is fine, you do not need the upper figure every day.

For example, an 80 kilogram lifter in muscle gain mode starts from 1.6 to 2.2 grams per kilogram. That converts to 128 to 176 grams per day, with a midpoint near 152 grams. At moderate activity the tool adds 0.1 gram per kilogram to each end, shifting the range to 136 to 184 grams. Spreading roughly 150 grams across four meals is easier than loading it into one sitting, and the target sits inside an overall eating plan rather than on top of unlimited calories.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Tip & Bill Split Calculator?
page.whatIs:
Answer first: a tip and bill split calculator takes the subtotal on a receipt, applies a tip rate, adds tax if you need it, and divides the total into equal shares. The arithmetic is simple, but the order matters, because tipping on the pre-tax amount and tipping on the post-tax amount give different numbers.

The tip is the bill multiplied by the tip rate as a decimal. A 15 percent tip on an 80.00 bill is 80.00 times 0.15, which is 12.00. Sales tax is a flat rate set locally. If tax is 8 percent, tax on that same bill is 6.40. The total to pay is bill plus tax plus tip, which here is 98.40. Splitting that total between four people gives 24.60 each.

This tool always works out the tip on the bill before tax. That follows the common habit of tipping on the service subtotal rather than on government tax. You can turn tax on with one switch, enter a single flat rate, and decide whether to round each share to the nearest whole currency unit. Rounding happens only after the division, so no one pays a fractional coin.

The split count accepts whole numbers from 1 to 100. With rounding on, the hero share is a whole number while the breakdown still shows the exact total, tax and tip. Presets cover 0, 15, 18 and 20 percent, and a custom rate handles anything else. Every calculation runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded.

page.exampleNote: Tip uses the 80.00 bill before tax. The 100.80 total is then split four ways with no rounding needed.
page.mistakes:
Tipping on the post-tax total::This tool tips on the bill before tax, as most people do, so a post-tax estimate will look higher.
Splitting before adding the tip::Divide only after tax and tip are included, or the collected amount will fall short.
Counting the wrong number of people::Include everyone sharing the bill, otherwise each share will be too large.
Rounding every share separately::Rounding each person can drift from the real total, so this tool rounds only the final share.
page.limits:

page.faqs:
Should I tip before or after tax?::This calculator works out the tip on the bill before tax, which is the usual convention for restaurant service. If your local practice is to tip on the after-tax total, add the tax rate to the tip rate mentally and enter the combined figure as a custom tip.
How is the per person share calculated?::The bill, tax and tip are added into one total, and that total is divided by the number of people you entered. The result is shown to two decimal places by default. Turn on rounding if you want a whole number that is easier to pay in cash.
What does the round per person option do?::It rounds the final share to the nearest whole currency unit after the division. The breakdown still shows the exact bill, tax, tip and total, and the rounded note tells you that the displayed share differs slightly from the precise figure.
Can I enter a tip that is not a preset?::Yes. Choose Custom in the tip control and type any rate from zero upward. The custom field uses the same decimal rules as the presets, so 17.5 means 17.5 percent. You can also set the rate to zero if no tip is needed.
page.trustBody: Calculates tip from the pre-tax bill, adds a flat tax rate and divides the total evenly. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to split a bill with tip and tax
page.guidance:
The Tip & Bill Split Calculator turns one subtotal into a tip, a grand total and an equal share for each person. Tip is worked out on the bill before tax, following the usual habit of tipping on the service amount rather than on government tax. Sales tax, when you switch it on, is a single flat rate added to that same subtotal. The total is bill plus tax plus tip, and the per person figure divides that total by your split count. Rounding happens only after the division, so the breakdown still shows exact currency figures.

Consider a dinner bill of 80.00 with an 18 percent tip, 8 percent sales tax and four people sharing. The tip comes to 14.40, tax is 6.40, and the total reaches 100.80, which works out at 25.20 each. If your local practice is to tip on the after-tax amount, add the two rates together and enter 26 percent as a custom tip instead. Counting every person at the table matters here, because leaving one diner out inflates everyone else's share.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Discount & Final Price Calculator?
page.whatIs:
Answer first: a discount and final price calculator subtracts a markdown from an original price, then adds any coupon and tax, to show what you actually pay. It also reports the savings in currency so you can judge whether a deal is as good as the advert claims.

There are two common ways to quote a discount. Percent off means a share of the price, so 25 percent off 200.00 saves 50.00 and leaves 150.00. Amount off means a fixed sum, so 50.00 off the same price also leaves 150.00. This tool accepts either form and converts a percent into an amount before doing anything else.

An extra coupon is taken off after the first discount. If the coupon is 20.00, the 150.00 becomes 130.00. Tax is then charged on that reduced price, not on the original price. At a 5 percent rate, tax is 6.50 and the final price is 136.50. Total savings are the first discount plus the coupon, which is 70.00 here.

When discounts and coupons together exceed the price, savings are capped at the price and the reduced price becomes zero. Percent discounts are limited to 100 percent, and an amount discount cannot be larger than the price. All figures are shown to two decimal places. Every calculation runs locally in your browser, so no price you enter is sent anywhere.

page.exampleInput:
Original price: 200.00
Discount: 25 percent
Coupon: 20.00
Sales tax: 5 percent
page.exampleOutput:
Discount: 50.00
Coupon: 20.00
Sales tax: 6.50
You save: 70.00
Final price: 136.50
page.exampleNote: Tax is charged on the 130.00 price after both discounts, which makes the final total 136.50.
page.howToTitle: How to use Discount & Final Price Calculator
page.howTo:

page.mistakes:
Applying tax before the discount::Real sales tax is charged on the reduced price. Applying it to the original price makes the final total too high.
Treating a coupon as a percent::The coupon field takes a fixed currency amount, so enter the value printed on the coupon rather than a rate.
Mixing up the two discount modes::Percent off uses a share of the price, while Amount off uses a fixed sum, so check the selected mode before typing.
Ignoring the savings cap::A combined discount and coupon larger than the price cannot make the item free and more, so savings stop at the price.
page.limits:
Savings are capped at the original price.
Tax is one flat rate on the discounted price.
Percent discounts are limited to 100 percent.
Prices are displayed to two decimal places.
page.faqs:
How is the final price calculated?::The tool turns the discount into a currency amount, subtracts it from the original price, then subtracts any coupon you entered. A single sales tax rate is applied to that reduced price, and the result is the final price. Savings are the discount plus the coupon, shown separately in the breakdown.
Is sales tax applied before or after the discount?::After. Retail tax is normally charged on the amount actually paid, so this tool taxes the price left after the markdown and the coupon. If a jurisdiction taxes the original price instead, you can enter that price tax as a coupon and set the tax rate to zero.
What happens if the coupon is bigger than the remaining price?::Savings are capped at the original price and the reduced price stops at zero. A short note appears under the result to explain the cap. You cannot get money back from the seller with this calculator, so the final price before tax stays at zero.
Can I use this for two successive percentage discounts?::Not as two separate steps, because this tool accepts one discount plus one fixed coupon. Convert the second percentage into an amount using the already reduced price, then enter that amount as the coupon. The tax step will still be applied after both reductions.
page.trustBody: Applies percent or fixed discounts, then a coupon and a flat tax rate on the reduced price. Updated 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to read your savings and final price
page.guidance:
The Discount & Final Price Calculator reports savings in currency alongside the checkout total after every reduction. Choose percent off when the markdown is quoted as a share of the price, or amount off when it is a fixed sum. The tool turns a percent into a currency amount first, subtracts it from the original price, then subtracts any coupon you add. Tax is charged on the reduced price rather than the original one, so the final price reflects what you actually pay. Total savings are the discount plus the coupon, shown separately from the tax line.

Take a jacket priced at 200.00 with 25 percent off, a 20.00 coupon and 5 percent sales tax. The discount removes 50.00, the coupon cuts another 20.00, and tax adds 6.50 on the 130.00 reduced price, leaving a final price of 136.50 with savings of 70.00. When comparing two offers, judge the currency saved rather than the headline percentage. A 30 percent markdown on a smaller item can easily save less than 20 percent off a larger one.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Profit Margin & Markup Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A profit margin and markup calculator separates three numbers that people often mix up: profit in currency, gross margin as a share of the selling price, and markup as a share of the cost. Start with two inputs, unit cost and selling price. Net profit is selling price minus cost. Gross margin percent is net profit divided by selling price, multiplied by 100. Markup percent is net profit divided by cost, multiplied by 100. Because the denominators differ, the same profit always produces a markup higher than its margin.

This tool also accepts a target. In margin mode the target is the gross margin you want, and the required price is cost divided by one minus the target as a decimal. In markup mode the target is markup on cost, and the required price is cost multiplied by one plus the target as a decimal. The gap line subtracts your entered selling price from that required price, so a positive gap means the current price falls short and a negative gap means it clears the target.

Three assumptions matter. Costs are treated as the full unit cost of the item, including any fees you choose to fold in. Selling price is the amount the customer actually pays before taxes that you pass through. Figures use exact arithmetic and are rounded to two decimal places for display; the underlying values keep more precision until that final step.

A margin of 100 percent requires an infinite price, so the tool rejects that target with a typed error. Zero cost or zero selling price also breaks the divisions, and both are reported instead of showing a misleading number. All arithmetic runs in your browser, with no upload and no account.
page.features:
Net profit::Selling price minus cost, shown in currency with a profit or loss label.
Gross margin::Profit as a percentage of the selling price, the figure investors usually quote.
Markup::Profit as a percentage of cost, the figure sellers use when setting a price.
Target price::The selling price needed to hit your chosen margin or markup target.
Gap to target::Required price minus your price, so you can see how far off the current price sits.
page.exampleInput:
Mode: Target margin
Cost: 40
Selling price: 60
Target: 30
page.exampleOutput:
Net profit: 20
Gross margin: 33.33%
Markup: 50%
Target price: 57.14
Gap to target: -2.86
page.exampleNote: The same 20 profit is 33.33 percent of the price but 50 percent of the cost. That difference is why margin and markup are never interchangeable.
page.mistakes:
Confusing margin with markup::A 50 percent markup is only a 33.33 percent margin when cost is 40 and price is 60. Always check the denominator.
Applying the target to cost in margin mode::Margin divides by price. Use markup mode if you mean a percentage added to cost.
Ignoring a negative gap::A negative gap means your price is above the target price, which is not the same as a loss. Check the profit label too.
Rounding the target price early::Keep two decimal places until the end, then round. Reusing a rounded price changes the margin slightly.
page.limits:
Cost and selling price must both be greater than zero.
A target margin of 100 percent is rejected because it needs an infinite price.
Targets above 1000 percent are rejected in markup mode.
Display values are rounded to two decimal places.
page.faqs:
What is the difference between margin and markup?::Margin is profit divided by selling price, while markup is profit divided by cost. With a cost of 40 and a price of 60, profit is 20, so margin is 33.33 percent and markup is 50 percent. The calculator shows both so you never confuse them.
How is the target price calculated?::In margin mode the tool divides cost by one minus the target written as a decimal, such as 40 divided by 0.7 for a 30 percent margin. In markup mode it multiplies cost by one plus the target. The gap line then compares that price with the one you entered.
Why did I get an error instead of a result?::The tool needs a finite, positive cost and selling price, because both divisions use them as denominators. A target margin of 100 percent is also invalid, since reaching it would require an infinite price. Each error includes a short hint that tells you which value to change.
Does the calculator include tax and shipping?::No. It treats the selling price as the amount the customer pays and cost as the unit cost you enter. If tax is passed straight through, leave it out of both fields. If shipping is a real cost to you, add it to cost before calculating.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Every figure is computed locally in your browser from the numbers you enter, with no upload and no account. Only your chosen mode is remembered between visits. Reviewed 26 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: Why margin and markup give different numbers
page.guidance:
Gross margin and markup both describe the same profit but divide by different bases, which is why the two never match. Gross margin divides profit by the selling price, the figure investors quote. Markup divides profit by unit cost, the figure sellers use when setting a price. Because cost is smaller than price, markup always reads higher than margin on the same sale. The target line goes further, showing the price needed to reach your chosen margin or markup and the gap between that price and the one you entered.

With a unit cost of 40 and a selling price of 60, profit is 20. That is a 33.33 percent margin but a 50 percent markup, so a request for a 50 percent margin does not mean a 50 percent markup. In margin mode the required price is cost divided by one minus the target written as a decimal, which gives 57.14 for a 30 percent margin here. A negative gap simply means your current price clears the target, not that you are losing money. Check the profit label.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Reading Time & Speaking Time Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A reading time and speaking time calculator converts a passage into two duration estimates by dividing its word count by a words per minute rate. The reading estimate uses a silent reading rate, commonly around 200 words per minute for general adult prose. The speaking estimate uses a slower rate, often near 130 words per minute for clear narration. Both results are rounded to the nearest second and shown as minutes and seconds.

Words are counted as runs of characters separated by whitespace, so hyphenated terms count as one word and numbers count as words. Character counts include every letter, digit, space and line break in the pasted text. A separate count removes all whitespace, which is useful when a layout has a strict character limit. Empty text produces zero words, so neither estimate shows a time.

The formula is simple: duration in minutes equals word count divided by the chosen rate. This tool multiplies by 60 and rounds to whole seconds, then splits the result into minutes and seconds. Rates are treated as constant for the whole passage. Real reading speed varies with difficulty, familiarity and purpose, so treat the numbers as planning estimates rather than precise predictions.

The tool assumes plain prose with no time spent on images, tables or code blocks. It caps pasted text at 100000 characters to keep the page responsive, and it rejects rates that are not positive finite numbers. All counting and arithmetic run locally in your browser, and your text is never uploaded or stored.

Speaking time::Word count divided by your speaking rate, usually longer than reading time.
Word count::Whitespace-separated runs, including numbers and hyphenated terms.
Character counts::Total characters and a total with all whitespace removed.

Using one rate for both figures::Speaking is slower than silent reading, so keep two different rates.
Treating the result as a promise::Difficulty and familiarity change real speed, especially with technical text.
Forgetting line breaks count::The character count includes spaces and line breaks. Use the no-space count for strict limits.
Pasting markup or tables::The tool counts them as words, which inflates the estimate for code heavy passages.

Times are rounded to the nearest whole second.
The tool does not account for images, tables or pauses.
page.faqs:
What reading speed does the calculator use?::It starts at 200 words per minute, a common planning figure for general adult prose. You can change it to match your own pace. The speaking speed starts at 130 words per minute, which is slower because saying words aloud takes longer than reading them silently.
How are words and characters counted?::Words are runs of characters separated by whitespace, so a hyphenated term counts as one word. Characters include letters, digits, spaces and line breaks. A second count removes all whitespace, which helps when a form or caption has a strict limit.
Why is speaking time longer than reading time?::The two estimates use different rates. Reading silently is usually faster than speaking clearly, so dividing the same word count by a smaller speaking rate gives a larger number of minutes. You can set both rates to whatever matches your situation.
Is my text stored or uploaded?::No. Counting and arithmetic run entirely in your browser, and the text stays on your device. Nothing is uploaded, and there is no account. The Clear button resets the passage and both rates, so a fresh session starts from the default values each time.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. All counting and timing happen locally in your browser, with no upload and no account. Your text is never saved. Reviewed 26 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How to estimate reading and speaking time
page.guidance:
The Reading Time & Speaking Time Calculator divides your word count by a words per minute rate to give two durations. Silent reading uses the faster rate, while speaking aloud uses a slower one, so the speaking time normally comes out longer. Both figures are rounded to the nearest second and shown as minutes and seconds. Words are counted as runs of characters separated by whitespace, so a hyphenated term counts as one word and a number counts as one too. Use the no-space character count for a strict layout limit.

A 600 word article at the default 200 words per minute takes about three minutes to read, while the same passage at 130 words per minute takes roughly four minutes and 37 seconds to say aloud. For a slide talk, set the speaking rate to your own measured pace and rehearse once against the estimate. Dense technical prose or passages with tables and code read more slowly than general prose, so raise the duration when planning a deadline rather than treating the number as a guarantee.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Calorie Deficit Timeline Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A calorie deficit timeline calculator estimates how long a weight change will take at a fixed daily energy gap. This tool takes a current weight, a target weight and a daily deficit or surplus, then converts the difference into weeks with a simple energy equation. A deficit means eating below maintenance to lose weight. A surplus means eating above maintenance to gain weight. The target must point in the same direction as the gap, otherwise the result would describe a plan that cannot work.

The arithmetic uses one common planning figure: one kilogram of body mass stores roughly 7700 kcal of energy. The energy gap is the absolute weight change multiplied by 7700. For an 8 kg loss at 500 kcal a day, that is 61600 kcal. Dividing by 500 gives 123.2 days, and dividing by seven gives about 17.6 weeks. The tool also reports the weekly rate, which is the daily gap times seven divided by 7700. At 500 kcal a day the rate is about 0.45 kg a week.

Those numbers are estimates, not promises. Real weight change includes water shifts, muscle loss or gain, adaptive metabolism and days when the gap slips. The pacing note sorts the weekly rate into four bands. Below 0.25 kg a week is slow, 0.25 to 0.5 is gentle, 0.5 to 1 is steady, and above 1 is aggressive for most people. Slower gaps are easier to maintain and tend to preserve more lean mass. Faster gaps raise hunger and fatigue and often lead to rebound.

If you do not know your daily burn, start with a TDEE estimate, then subtract your chosen deficit or add your surplus. Everything here runs in your browser and no weight entry is stored.

page.howTo:

Set a target weight above or below it.
Choose deficit to lose weight or surplus to gain weight.
Enter the daily calorie gap you can sustain.
Read the weeks, weekly rate and pacing note.
Copy the plan for your records.

Current weight: 82 kg
Target weight: 74 kg
Daily mode: Deficit
Daily gap: 500 kcal
page.exampleOutput:

Estimated days: 123
Weight to change: 8.0 kg
Total energy gap: 61600 kcal
Change per week: 0.45 kg
page.exampleNote: This uses the flat 7700 kcal per kilogram estimate. Real results vary from week to week.
page.mistakes:
Assuming a fixed daily burn::Your maintenance changes as you lose or gain weight, so review the gap every few weeks.
Ignoring water weight::Scale changes in the first week are often water, not fat.
Choosing an extreme gap::Very large deficits raise hunger and fatigue and are hard to keep.
Treating weeks as a promise::Illness, sleep and training all change real progress.
page.limits:
Weights are limited to 30 to 300 kg.
The daily gap accepts 0 to 2000 kcal.
The model assumes one flat 7700 kcal per kilogram.
Results are planning estimates and not medical advice.
page.faqs:
How does this calculator estimate weeks?::It multiplies the weight change by 7700 kcal per kilogram, divides by your daily gap to get days, then divides by seven for weeks. The tool also shows the weekly rate so you can judge whether the pace is sustainable.
Why does my target need to match the deficit or surplus?::A deficit means intake is below burn, so weight moves down and the target must be lower. A surplus means intake is above burn, so the target must be higher. A mismatched pair would describe a plan that cannot produce the change you set.
What is a realistic weekly rate?::A rate near half a kilogram a week is a common planning target and is usually easier to sustain than a large gap. The pacing note flags slow, gentle, steady and aggressive rates so you can choose a gap you can actually keep.
Is 7700 kcal per kilogram exact?::No. It is a round planning figure for the energy stored in body mass. Real change includes water, muscle and metabolic adaptation, and the gap drifts as your weight moves. Treat the weeks as a rough guide and adjust with a food and weight log.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Uses a flat 7700 kcal per kilogram estimate and a four band pacing guide. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How Long Will My Calorie Deficit Take?
page.guidance:
A calorie deficit timeline answers how many weeks a weight change needs at a fixed daily energy gap. The calculator multiplies the kilograms you want to lose or gain by 7700 kcal per kilogram, divides that total by your daily gap to get days, then divides by seven for weeks. Read the weekly rate too: it shows whether the plan is sustainable, not just how soon the target arrives. A 500 kcal daily deficit toward an 8 kg goal gives roughly 17.6 weeks and about 0.45 kg per week.

Use the weekly rate to pick a gap you can hold rather than the shortest timeline. A rate near 0.5 kg a week, about 550 kcal a day, is a common planning target and is usually easier to sustain than a larger gap. If the tool shows more than 1 kg a week, trim the deficit because hunger and fatigue tend to end those plans early. Recheck the numbers every few weeks, since maintenance changes as your weight moves and water shifts can hide fat loss in the first week.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Drink & Beverage Calories Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A drink calories calculator estimates the energy in a beverage from its calorie density and the amount you drink. This tool bundles a small table of common soft drinks, juices, energy drinks, smoothies and alcoholic drinks. Each row stores typical calories per 100 ml and a common serving size. You pick a category, pick a drink, then adjust the millilitres and the number of servings.

The arithmetic is one product. Calories per serving equal calories per 100 ml multiplied by serving size in millilitres and divided by 100. Total calories are that figure multiplied by the number of servings. A cola with 43 kcal per 100 ml in a 330 ml can works out to about 142 kcal. Two cans give about 284 kcal. The same rule applies to every row, so a 150 ml glass of red wine at 85 kcal per 100 ml comes to roughly 128 kcal. Bottled drinks often list energy per 100 ml on the label, which makes the comparison straightforward.

The table uses rounded reference values. Sugar free energy drinks sit near zero, while smoothies and cocktails are much denser because of fruit, yogurt or spirits. Serving sizes are typical, not legal definitions, and a cafe or bar may pour a larger amount. Alcohol also carries energy that is not tracked as carbohydrate, so the figure reflects total calories rather than macros.

Everything runs in your browser. The breakdown shows the density, serving size, count, per serving calories and the total, and you can copy the whole thing as plain text.

How are drink calories calculated?::Each drink has a typical calorie value per 100 ml. The tool multiplies that by your serving size in millilitres, divides by 100, then multiplies by the number of servings. The breakdown shows every step and the final total.
Why use calories per 100 ml?::It makes drinks easy to compare even when containers differ. A label that lists energy per 100 ml can be entered directly, and changing the serving size updates the total without switching drinks or rebuilding the calculation.
Are smoothie and cocktail values reliable?::They are rough estimates. Recipes vary widely, and a smoothie with yogurt or a cocktail with syrup can be much denser than the table value. Use the number to compare choices, then check a label or recipe when you need precision.
Does the tool track sugar or alcohol separately?::No. It reports total calories from the bundled per 100 ml values. Sugar free drinks sit near zero, while alcoholic drinks include the energy from alcohol itself. For macros or a specific brand, read the package label.

Use the per 100 ml figure to compare choices before you order. page.whatIsTitle: What is a Walking & Running Calories Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A walking and running calories calculator turns movement into an energy estimate by combining body weight, pace and either distance or duration. This tool uses the MET method: energy in kilocalories equals MET multiplied by body weight in kilograms and by time in hours. MET is a metabolic equivalent that compares an activity with sitting quietly, so a higher pace raises the multiplier.

Enter your weight in kilograms or pounds. Pounds are converted with the factor 0.45359237 kilograms per pound. Choose kilometers or miles for distance and pace, and the tool converts miles with 1.609344 kilometers per mile. In distance mode, time comes from distance multiplied by pace. In duration mode, distance comes from time divided by pace. Either way, pace sets the speed used to look up a MET value.

The MET tables use walking values from about 2.8 at a slow 3 km/h stroll up to 8.0 for a fast 8 km/h race walk, and running values from about 6.5 at 6 km/h up to 15.0 at a fast 16 km/h run. Values between table points are interpolated and extreme speeds are clamped, which keeps odd inputs from producing wild results. For a 70 kilogram walker at 5 km/h for 60 minutes, the MET is 4.3 and the estimate is about 301 kcal.

The figure is gross energy, so it includes the calories you would have burned sitting still during that hour. Actual burn varies with fitness, body composition, hills, surface, wind and how accurately you record pace. Treat the number as a planning estimate, not a measurement, and use a heart rate monitor or lab test when precision matters.

Copy the result to keep the estimate.
page.features:
Two input modes::Distance or duration, with the missing value calculated from your pace.
Pace aware MET::Walking and running use separate lookup tables with interpolation.
Unit switching::Kilometers or miles for distance and pace, kilograms or pounds for weight.
Gross energy estimate::The result includes resting burn and is rounded to whole kcal.
Plain text report::Copy weight, pace, time, distance, speed and MET in one step.
page.mistakes:
Counting gross as net::The MET result includes resting energy, so it is higher than an active only figure.
Mixing pace units::Keep distance and pace in the same unit or the speed will be wrong.
Ignoring terrain::Hills, wind and rough ground change energy use more than pace alone suggests.
page.limits:
Walking speed is expected between 3 and 8 km/h and running between 6 and 16 km/h.
Weights outside 1 to 400 kg or 2 to 900 lb are rejected.
The result is an estimate, not medical or nutrition advice.
page.faqs:
How are walking calories calculated?::The tool multiplies a MET value by your weight in kilograms and by the time in hours. Your pace sets the speed, and the speed looks up a MET from separate walking and running tables. The total is gross energy, which includes resting burn.
Can I enter time instead of distance?::Yes. Switch to duration mode and enter the number of minutes you moved. Add your usual pace, and the calculator works out the distance from time and pace, then uses the same MET table to estimate energy. The speed and distance appear in the breakdown.
Does the tool handle miles and pounds?::Yes. Choose miles for distance and pace, or pounds for weight, and the calculator converts them with standard factors before doing the arithmetic. Miles use 1.609344 kilometers each and pounds use 0.45359237 kilograms each, so the MET lookup always works in kilometers per hour.
Why is my estimate different from a watch?::Watches combine step counts, heart rate and personal data, while this tool uses only weight, pace and time. Hills, wind, surface, fitness and stride efficiency can shift real energy use by a wide margin. Use the number to compare options and plan, not as a precise reading.
page.trustBody: Walking and running estimates use published MET ranges with linear interpolation between table points. All arithmetic runs in your browser, and only your preferred units are remembered. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How Many Calories Does a Walk Burn?
page.guidance:
Walking and running calories are estimated with the MET method: energy in kcal equals MET multiplied by body weight in kilograms and time in hours. Your pace sets the speed, and the speed looks up a MET from separate walking and running tables, with values between points interpolated. A 70 kg walker at 5 km/h for 60 minutes uses a MET of 4.3 and burns about 301 kcal. That figure is gross energy, so it includes the calories you would have burned sitting still for the same hour.

Use the estimate to compare options rather than to track a precise burn. Enter either distance or minutes plus your usual pace; the calculator solves for the other value and shows speed and intensity so a brisk walk can be checked against a slow run. Hills, wind, surface and stride efficiency change real energy use more than pace alone suggests, so treat the number as a planning figure. If you are adding movement to a food budget, keep the net gain conservative because the gross figure already counts resting burn.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Recipe Serving Scaler Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A recipe serving scaler multiplies every ingredient amount by one factor so a dish fits a different number of servings. This tool reads one ingredient per line, finds a leading quantity when there is one, multiplies it and writes the new amount back in place. Text without a leading number, such as salt to taste, is copied unchanged.

You can scale in two ways. Enter the recipe's original servings and the servings you want, and the factor is desired divided by original. Or press a multiplier chip for half, single, double or triple batch. The chips set the desired servings for you, and typing a new serving count clears the chip selection.

Amounts come back as readable fractions where possible. Values near one half, one third, two thirds, one quarter, three quarters, one eighth or their common mixed forms use fraction characters. Anything that does not land near a clean fraction is shown as a decimal with at most two places. A quantity of 1.5 cups at double becomes 3 cups, while 0.5 teaspoon at triple becomes 1.5 teaspoons, shown as one and a half.

The tool only scales the first number on each line. Ranges, oven temperatures and times are not adjusted, so read the result before cooking. Pan sizes and cooking times rarely scale in a straight line, and spices often need less than a pure multiple when a recipe grows. Use the copyable recipe as a starting point and adjust by taste.

page.exampleInput:
Original servings: 4
Desired servings: 6

1/2 cup diced onion
1 1/2 tbsp olive oil
Salt and pepper to taste
page.exampleOutput:
Scale factor: 1.5
3 cups vegetable broth
¾ cup diced onion
2¼ tbsp olive oil
Salt and pepper to taste
page.exampleNote: Only the leading amount changes. Text lines and units stay as written.

page.mistakes:
Scaling every number::The tool changes the first number on a line, so times and temperatures stay untouched on purpose.
Rounding too early::Fractions are kept where they are clean, which avoids cumulative rounding across ingredients.
Expecting linear spice growth::Strong spices often need less than a straight multiple when you double a batch.
page.limits:
One ingredient per line is required for clean parsing.
Servings outside 1 to 100 original or 1 to 200 desired are rejected.
Pan sizes and cook times are not adjusted.
page.faqs:
How does the scaler change ingredient amounts?::It finds the first number on each ingredient line, multiplies it by your factor and writes the result back with its original unit and text. Amounts near a clean fraction use fraction characters, while other amounts use a decimal with up to two places.
What if a line has no number?::Lines such as salt to taste or a note about preparation are copied through unchanged. The scaled list keeps the same line order as your input, so you can compare the original and the result side by side before you copy it.
Can I scale by multiplier instead of servings?::Yes. The half, single, double and triple chips set the desired servings from your original count instantly. If you later type a different serving number, no chip stays selected and the factor is recalculated from the two serving values.
Are cooking times and pan sizes scaled too?::No. Only ingredient quantities change. Cooking time, oven temperature and pan size depend on volume and surface area, so they do not scale in a straight line. Read the scaled recipe and adjust those details by experience and by watching the food.

page.guidanceTitle: How Do I Resize a Recipe by Servings?
page.guidance:
A recipe scaler resizes every ingredient by one factor so the dish fits a different yield. Enter the servings the recipe was written for and the servings you want, and the factor is desired divided by original. The tool changes only the first number on each line, keeps the unit and the rest of the text, and returns clean fractions where they land near a half, third, quarter or eighth, otherwise a decimal with two places. Lines without a leading amount, such as salt to taste, pass through unchanged.

Scaling from four servings to six gives a factor of 1.5, so 2 cups of broth becomes 3 cups and 1/2 cup of onion becomes 3/4 cup. Use the multiplier chips when you want a half, double or triple batch without typing new serving counts; typing a count clears the chip. Read the result before cooking, because oven temperature, cooking time and pan size do not change with volume, and strong spices often need less than a straight multiple when a batch grows.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Freelance Hourly Rate Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A freelance hourly rate calculator starts with the income you want to keep and works backward to a price you can charge. The core formula is: required revenue = (target net income + annual expenses) / (1 - tax and buffer rate as a decimal). Divide that revenue by your total billable hours for the year, which is billable weeks multiplied by billable hours per week, and you have a baseline hourly rate.

The daily rate takes that hourly figure and multiplies it by the hours you can bill in one day, estimated as weekly billable hours divided by billable days per week. The project rate multiplies the hourly figure by the number of hours in a typical project. Keeping all three rates tied to one hourly baseline means a day or a project never quietly undercuts your target.

Three assumptions matter. First, target net income is what you keep after expenses and tax, not gross revenue. Second, the tax and buffer field is a single combined percentage of revenue, so a rate of 25 means you set aside a quarter of every invoice. Third, billable time is not the same as working time. Admin, sales and holidays belong outside the billable count, which is why the sample uses 46 weeks and 30 hours rather than a full calendar.

The tool rounds the displayed rates to two decimal places but keeps full precision until the final step. A tax and buffer value of 100 percent or more is rejected because no revenue would remain as income. Zero billable weeks, hours or days are also rejected since they would make the division impossible. Everything runs locally in your browser.

Add the weeks and hours you can actually bill, plus billable days per week.

How do I choose a freelance hourly rate?::Start with the income you need to keep, add yearly expenses and gross that total up for tax and savings. Divide by the hours you can realistically bill. This tool does that arithmetic and shows hourly, daily and project rates so you can quote consistently.
Why is my daily rate lower than I expected?::The daily rate uses billable hours per day, which this tool estimates from your weekly billable hours divided by billable days per week. If you bill 30 hours across five days, a day is six billable hours, not eight. Reduce the days per week to raise the daily figure.
What does the tax and buffer percentage mean?::It is one combined share of every invoice that you set aside for tax and savings. Enter 25 and the tool assumes 75 percent of revenue remains as take-home income, so required revenue is divided by 0.75. Values of 100 or more are rejected.
Should I bill by the hour, day or project?::Use the hourly rate for ongoing work, the daily rate for short engagements and the project rate for a fixed scope. All three come from the same baseline, so switching between them will not change what you earn as long as the hours are accurate.
