page.faqs:
Where are the salt and initialization vector stored?::Both are written into the payload next to the ciphertext. They are not secret. Keeping them with the message means the receiving side can rebuild the key and decrypt without a separate exchange. A new pair is generated for every encryption, so the same message encrypted twice will produce two different payloads.
Can I decrypt with a different passphrase?::No. The derived key will not match and the authentication check will fail, so the tool reports that the text could not be decrypted. There is no shortcut that recovers the original phrase from the payload. Keep a reliable record of the passphrase, because a lost phrase means the message cannot be opened again.
What happens if I edit one character of the payload?::AES-GCM includes an authentication tag, so any change to the salt, vector or ciphertext causes verification to fail. You will see a clear failure message rather than corrupted text. If that happens, ask for a fresh copy of the complete string and check that no line breaks or spaces were added when it was pasted.
Is this a messaging app?::No. It is a local text tool that encrypts and decrypts in your browser. It does not manage contacts, deliver messages or store keys. You decide how to share the payload and the passphrase, and you should send them through separate channels so one intercepted message does not reveal both pieces.
Does my text get uploaded?::No. Encryption and decryption run with Web Crypto in the browser tab. There is no network request, no account and no history of past messages. Clearing the tool removes the text from the visible fields, and closing the tab ends the session. The output is plain text you can copy or download yourself.
Why is the output longer than the message?::Base64 encoding expands binary data, and the payload also carries a version label, salt, initialization vector and authentication tag. Short messages therefore produce a noticeably longer string. That extra data is what makes independent encryption and reliable verification possible without any stored settings.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a PBKDF2 hash generator?
page.whatIs:
A PBKDF2 hash generator turns a passphrase into a fixed length key by repeating a pseudorandom function many times. This workspace uses PBKDF2 with SHA-256 through the Web Crypto API. A fresh random salt is created for every hash, and the iteration count controls how much work each derivation takes. Although the route keeps its original name, the algorithm used here is PBKDF2 and not bcrypt.

The output is a single portable string with four parts separated by dollar signs: the algorithm label, the iteration count, the salt and the derived digest. Storing those values together means the same string can be verified later without keeping a separate settings file. The salt does not need to be secret. Its job is to make identical passphrases produce different stored values and to block precomputed lookup tables.

Verification reverses the process without recovering the passphrase. The tool reads the salt and rounds from the saved string, derives a new digest from the phrase you enter, and compares it with the stored digest using a length aware constant work comparison. A match means the phrase is the same one used to create the hash. There is no way to read the original text back out of the stored value.

Everything runs in this browser tab. The passphrase is never transmitted, and no hash is written to a server. Rounds can be raised as hardware gets faster, because a higher count makes each guess more expensive. Choose a count your devices can handle, keep the stored string somewhere safe, and treat each hash as specific to one account or purpose.

page.guidanceTitle: Choosing rounds and storing hashes
page.guidance:
Pick an iteration count that makes a single derivation noticeably slow on an ordinary device but still comfortable for your workflow. A higher count raises the cost of every guess an attacker makes, so it is the main dial available when hardware improves. The random salt is equally important: each new hash gets its own, so two accounts with the same phrase produce different stored values. Keep the whole string together when you save it, because the rounds and salt are needed for a later check.

When verifying, paste the complete string rather than only the digest. The tool reads the settings from the stored value, so a missing field cannot be checked and a specific hint appears instead. A match confirms the phrase is unchanged, while a failure means the phrase or the stored string differs. A derived key cannot be reversed into readable text, so keep a separate recovery method for any passphrase you cannot afford to lose. No value is sent off this device at any point.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a chmod calculator?
page.whatIs:
Unix file permissions are stored as three sets of bits. One set describes the owner, one the group, and one everyone else. Each set can grant read, write and execute access independently, which gives eight possible states per set and a compact three digit mode.

The numeric form uses four as read, two as write and one as execute. Adding the granted bits gives a digit from zero to seven. A common web directory mode is 0755, meaning the owner can write while everyone can read and enter the directory.

The symbolic form writes the same state as nine characters. Three letters per class record read, write and execute, with a dash where access is denied. The first character in a full listing describes the file type, so a mode string usually appears as rwxr-xr-x.

This calculator keeps both forms in sync. Toggling a checkbox rebuilds the octal and symbolic strings and a copyable chmod command. You can go the other way by entering a three digit octal value. Special bits such as setuid and sticky are outside this three digit view.

page.howTo:

page.guidanceTitle: Choosing sensible permission modes for files
page.guidance:
Start with the narrowest mode that still works. A private document usually needs 0600, which gives the owner read and write access and nothing to anyone else. A public web page is normally 0644, and a directory that must be entered is usually 0755. Write access for the public is rarely appropriate.

Read the symbolic string as a final check before copying. Three rwx blocks should match what you intended for owner, group and public, and any dash marks a denied right. When you paste an octal value, the calculator fills the checkboxes so you can inspect the result rather than trusting the digits alone. Keep a record of the mode you applied so a later audit has useful context for each file.

Why is the symbolic string nine characters?::There are three classes of user and three rights for each class. Each right is shown as its letter or a dash, so three groups of three characters describe the whole mode. A full directory listing adds one leading character for the file type before those nine.
Can I enter a mode directly?::Yes. Type a three digit octal value such as 644 or 755 and press Apply. The calculator fills all nine toggles so you can inspect the rights before copying a command. Values outside the octal range are rejected with a message that explains the accepted format.

Does this work for Windows files?::Windows uses a different access model, so these octal modes do not apply to a local NTFS file. They matter on Unix-like systems, including Linux and macOS, and in containers or deployment scripts. Use the symbolic string to explain a mode to a teammate.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a CSS gradient generator?

A CSS gradient generator writes a background image value from a small set of choices. A linear gradient blends colours along a line you control with an angle, while a radial gradient blends outward from a point. In both cases the browser draws the pixels, so the result stays sharp at any size.

Colour stops define the recipe. Each stop holds a colour and a percentage that says where that colour reaches full strength. The browser interpolates between neighbouring stops. Two stops make a simple blend, and extra stops let you band a transition or reproduce a brand palette precisely.

Angles follow CSS convention: zero points upward and ninety degrees points right. The radial controls place the origin at the centre, the top edge or the top left corner. Stops are sorted by position in the output, so adding one in the middle does not change the visual order.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a CSS shadow generator?
page.whatIs:
A CSS shadow generator turns a handful of numeric controls into a valid box-shadow value. The X and Y offsets move the shadow, blur softens its edge, spread grows or shrinks its footprint, and colour sets the tint. An inset flag draws the shadow inside the element instead of outside.

The box-shadow property accepts several layers separated by commas, painted from the first layer down to the last. Each layer here is built independently and joined in the order shown.

Colours are stored as hexadecimal values with a separate opacity percentage. The generator converts them to rgba so a soft shadow can let the page background show through. Native colour inputs keep the picker familiar, and the numeric bounds prevent extreme values from producing unusable output.

The preview card uses the same declaration that appears in the CSS box, so what you see is what you copy. There is no build step, no library and no server round trip. The sample button loads a three layer stack that demonstrates diffuse depth, a contact shadow and an inset light edge.

Each shadow layer has its own horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur, spread, inset flag and color. Positive offsets move the shadow right and down, blur softens the edge, and spread grows or shrinks the shape before blurring. Inset shadows are drawn inside the box, which is useful for pressed buttons and wells.

Layers are combined in the order shown, so the first layer sits in front. The live preview applies the same CSS string that appears in the output panel. Start from the sample, change one layer at a time, and copy the CSS when the depth feels right.

page.guidance:

Stacking two or three layers usually reads better than one heavy shadow because each layer can carry a different softness. Leave spread at zero unless you want the outline to grow evenly in every direction.

Keep opacity low on dark surfaces and slightly higher on light ones, since the same rgba value looks different against each background. Inset layers work best as a one pixel highlight along the top edge rather than a full inner shadow. Press Try sample to see this arrangement, then tune the numbers until the card sits comfortably in your layout.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an EXIF Metadata Remover?
page.whatIs:
Photographs can carry extra information beyond the visible pixels. Camera models, timestamps, GPS coordinates and editing software are often stored in EXIF blocks inside JPEG files, while PNG and WebP have their own chunk systems. A quick scanner can count known signatures, but reading every tag needs a full parser.

This tool inspects the ordinary file facts the browser exposes: name, MIME type, byte size and last modified time. If you enable the byte scan, it searches the raw bytes for JPEG APP1 EXIF headers, PNG eXIf chunks and WebP EXIF chunks, then reports how many signatures it found. That count is a hint, not a complete inventory.

Removing metadata works by drawing the decoded image onto a fresh canvas and encoding a new blob. The new file contains only pixel data and the headers the encoder adds itself. JPEG, PNG and WebP output are offered, and lossy quality applies to JPEG and WebP. The preview and before and after sizes come from the same local file.

Re encoding always changes the byte structure, and a lossy format can change pixel values slightly. If you need exact archival preservation, keep the original file. The 20 MB ceiling exists because decoding and canvas encoding both happen in memory on your device.

The metadata scan looks for common EXIF markers in the file bytes and reports what it finds. It is a basic scan, not a full EXIF parser, so specialist fields in unusual files may not be listed. Re-encoding through canvas removes embedded metadata because the new image is drawn from pixels rather than copied from the original byte stream.

Choosing a format changes the trade off. PNG keeps transparency and pixel accuracy, JPEG produces smaller photos but fills transparency with a background color, and WebP offers a useful middle ground. The result card compares byte sizes so you can see how much data was removed along with the metadata. The original file never leaves the browser.
page.howToTitle: How to use EXIF Metadata Remover
page.howTo:
Drop a JPEG, PNG or WebP file or choose one with the file picker.

page.guidanceTitle: What a byte scan can and cannot tell you
page.guidance:
Treat the signature count as a quick check, not a verdict. It tells you whether common EXIF markers are present in the raw bytes, so zero is reassuring but not a proof that every tag is gone. A full metadata reader would need to walk each container format and decode its tag structure.

Choose PNG when you want lossless pixels and transparency, JPEG for a compact photograph, and WebP when you want compression with an alpha channel. Re encoding is the only way to guarantee the new file starts clean, so expect the size to change. Keep the original if you need the exact byte stream for an archive. The before and after figures make that difference easy to see at a glance.

page.faqs:
Does this read every EXIF tag?::No. The byte scan counts a few known signatures such as JPEG APP1 EXIF headers and PNG eXIf chunks. It does not decode individual tags. A dedicated metadata reader is needed for a full inventory, and even then the safest way to produce a clean copy is re encoding.
Why does the file size change?::A clean copy is built from the decoded pixels and encoded again, so container headers are rebuilt. Lossless PNG can grow, while JPEG and WebP often shrink. The size comparison shows the exact difference, and the saved percentage is calculated from the two byte counts.
Will pixels stay identical?::PNG keeps the pixel values exactly because it is lossless. JPEG and WebP use lossy compression, so a second encoding can shift a few values slightly. If byte for byte preservation matters, keep the original file and use the clean copy only for sharing.
Can GPS coordinates survive?::Re encoding drops the metadata blocks that hold GPS fields because the new canvas holds only pixels. The scan looks for signatures, not individual GPS tags, so use it as a quick signal. For sensitive workflows, verify the downloaded file with a dedicated metadata tool.
Why is there a 20 MB ceiling?::The browser must hold the decoded image and the new canvas in memory at the same time. Very large files can exhaust that budget and fail on smaller devices. Convert or compress the photo first, then run the clean copy step on the reduced file.
Is my photo uploaded?::No. The file stays in this tab. The facts come from the file object, the byte scan reads its buffer locally, and the clean image is drawn on a canvas built here. The download uses a temporary object URL that is released when you reset.
Does the scan find every metadata field?::No. The scan checks for common EXIF markers in the file bytes and reports what it recognises. It is a basic inspector, not a full EXIF parser. Re-encoding still rebuilds the image from pixels, which removes embedded metadata that the simple scan may not name.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Fancy Text Generator?
page.whatIs:
A fancy text generator swaps ordinary letters for look-alike Unicode characters. The result looks like a different font, but it is still plain text: no stylesheet, image or download is involved. Paste a word into this tool and you receive versions such as bold, italic, monospace, strikethrough and script, each ready to copy.

These styles exist because Unicode includes several alphabets and decorative symbol blocks. Mathematical bold letters, script capitals, monospaced forms and combining strike marks are ordinary code points, so most apps accept them in a bio, display name, chat message or creative header. They travel with the text when you paste it somewhere else, which is why they are popular where a small change of shape makes a line stand out.

The trade-off is meaning and compatibility. Screen readers usually announce the underlying code point, so a sentence written entirely in script or decorative symbols may be read as symbol names instead of words. Search boxes, login forms, tags and accessibility tooling often expect plain letters, so stylised text can fail a lookup or a validation rule. Some older fonts omit decorative blocks and show empty boxes in their place.

This generator runs only in your browser. It maps each Latin letter and digit with a fixed table, so the same input always produces the same output and your words are never sent anywhere. Every preview updates as you type, and each card copies its exact string in one click.

page.guidance:

Pick the style that matches the tone of the line, copy it, and check the result inside the app where it will appear. Different platforms draw Unicode symbol blocks with different fonts, so a style that looks crisp in one app may fall back to boxes in another.

Keep styled strings brief so they stay easy to scan and paste. Screen readers often announce the underlying code point rather than the letter, which means a long passage in script or strikethrough may be read as symbols. Keep login fields, search boxes, labels and instructions in plain letters so they remain searchable and accessible. This generator maps Latin letters and digits only; punctuation and other scripts pass through unchanged, which keeps names and sentences readable.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a GPA Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A grade point average converts letter grades into numbers and weights them by credits. On the common four point scale an A is worth four points, a B is worth three, a C is worth two, a D is worth one and an F is worth zero, with plus and minus grades sitting between those values. Multiplying each grade value by its credits gives quality points, and dividing the total quality points by total credits gives the average.

This calculator separates the current term from earlier study. The semester figure uses only the rows you enter now. The cumulative figure combines this term with a prior average and prior credit total, recovering earlier quality points by multiplication. Both fields must be supplied together; when they are blank, the cumulative average matches the semester average.

An optional weighted mode adds half a point for honors courses and one point for advanced placement courses, with each course capped at five points. Many schools use a scale like this to recognise harder classes. Other schools do not, so the switch should follow the scale printed on your transcript rather than personal preference.

Every calculation runs locally in the browser. Course rows can be added or removed, and the result pane reports semester and cumulative averages, credits, quality points and the course count so the arithmetic can be checked line by line.

page.guidanceTitle: Reading Semester and Cumulative GPA
page.guidance:
A semester average describes one term, while the cumulative figure blends that term with the credits and grades you have already earned. Enter prior average and prior credits together; leaving one blank tells the tool to treat the history as empty. Check that credit values match your transcript, because a four credit course carries twice the influence of a two credit course.

Weighted scales change the value of each course. Honors rows add half a point and advanced placement rows add a full point, with each course capped at five points. Schools set their own rules, so use the weighted switch only when your transcript follows that convention. The result pane keeps both averages beside total credits and quality points, which makes it easier to explain the number to a registrar or an adviser.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an HTML entity encoder?
page.whatIs:
An HTML entity encoder replaces characters that have a special role in markup with reference strings. An ampersand becomes a named or numeric reference, and the same happens to the angle brackets that open and close tags. The browser then renders the original character instead of treating it as code.

This tool covers the five references used most often in text and attributes: ampersand, left angle bracket, right angle bracket, double quote and apostrophe. Encode mode converts those characters, while decode mode converts the references back. Named output uses short words such as amp and lt. Numeric output uses decimal character codes such as 38 and 60.

The ampersand is replaced first so an existing reference is not encoded a second time. Output updates as you type, and the replacement count shows how many characters changed. When decoding, a named reference outside the supported set is left untouched and a short warning explains what to do.

Everything happens in this tab. No text is sent to a server, so the tool is safe for drafts, templates and content that is not ready to share. For the official list of character references, see the trusted reference linked in the About this tool section.

page.guidanceTitle: How to choose an entity style
page.guidance:

Named output is easier to read in source code, while numeric output is safer in older pipelines that only understand decimal references. Decode mode turns those references back into the original characters for display or debugging.

The tool covers ampersand, left and right angle bracket, double quote and apostrophe. It replaces the ampersand first so existing references are not encoded twice. If a named reference outside this set appears during decoding, the result keeps it unchanged and shows a short warning with a fix hint. Check the replacement count before copying, then paste the output into your page or configuration.

Which characters does the tool encode?::It handles the ampersand, the left and right angle bracket, the double quote and the apostrophe. These are the characters that most often change meaning inside HTML text and attributes. Other characters are passed through unchanged, which keeps the output easy to read and predictable for the cases this tool is designed for.
What is the difference between named and numeric output?::Named output uses short words such as amp for an ampersand and lt for a left angle bracket. Numeric output uses the decimal character code, such as 38 or 60. Both render the same character in a browser. Named output is easier to scan, while numeric output works in simpler parsers that do not know the names.
Why replace the ampersand first?::Every other reference begins with an ampersand. If the parser encoded that character last, an existing reference would be escaped again and the reader would see the raw reference text. Encoding the ampersand first guarantees that each original character is handled exactly once and the result stays correct.
What happens to unknown named references?::During decoding, references outside the supported set are left as written and a short warning names the first one. This avoids silently changing content you may still need. Replace the reference with a supported entity, or keep it as plain text, then decode again to see the cleaned result in the output pane.
Does the tool send my text anywhere?::No. Encoding and decoding both run in this tab using local code. There is no network request and no stored copy of your input. The result stays on screen until you copy it or replace the text, making the tool suitable for private drafts and unreleased content.
Can I decode numeric references?::Yes. Decimal references such as 38 and hexadecimal references such as 0x26 are both understood, provided they form a valid character code. The replacement count tells you how many references were restored. Invalid or incomplete references are left untouched so that the surrounding text remains intact.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an Image Color Picker?
page.whatIs:
A color palette is a short list of shades that represent an image. Instead of choosing colors by eye, sampling groups similar pixels and ranks the groups by how often they appear. The result is a compact summary of the visual mood, useful when a design needs to match a photograph.

This tool draws the image onto a small canvas and reads its pixel data. Pixels are grouped into buckets, transparent pixels are skipped, and the most frequent buckets become swatches. Each swatch shows a HEX code, an RGB triple and an HSL triple, plus the share of sampled pixels it represents.

HEX is compact for CSS, RGB describes the red, green and blue channels, and HSL describes hue, saturation and lightness. Seeing all three makes it easier to adjust a shade by hand. The CSS block writes each color as a custom property, so the palette can be pasted into a theme file.

Sampling is approximate by design. A bucket may blend nearby shades, and a dominant background can crowd out small accent colors. Changing the palette size reveals more or fewer groups. The image never leaves the tab, and the sample button builds a test strip locally so the flow can be tried instantly.

Color extraction reads the pixels of the uploaded image directly. Fully transparent pixels are ignored, and the remaining samples are grouped into color buckets so the displayed HEX values reflect what is actually visible. A lower color count merges similar shades, while a higher count reveals small accents.

Each swatch shows its HEX, RGB and HSL values plus the share of sampled pixels it represents. The CSS block maps the palette to custom properties with simple names, ready to paste into a stylesheet. Because the palette comes from your own image, the result is a real palette rather than a decorative preset.

page.guidanceTitle: Reading a palette you can actually use
page.guidance:
A palette is a starting point, not a finished theme. The most common swatch is often a background or a large flat area, so look further down the list for accents that carry the character of the image. The share percentage helps you tell a dominant tone from a small highlight that still matters.

Use HEX for quick CSS edits, RGB when a tool expects channel values, and HSL when you need to lift lightness or shift hue without changing the other two. The custom property block drops straight into a root rule. For accessible text, test the chosen color against its background before you commit to it in a component. A quick contrast check saves a lot of rework later.

How are the colors chosen?::The image is drawn small on a canvas and its pixels are grouped into buckets of similar values. Buckets are ranked by how often they occur, and the top groups become swatches. Transparent pixels are ignored, and each swatch is the average color of its bucket.
Why can a small accent be missing?::Ranking favours area, so a tiny bright detail can lose to a large flat background. Increase the palette size to reveal smaller groups. If an accent still does not appear, crop the image around that detail first and sample again.
What does the share percentage mean?::It is the share of sampled pixels that fell into that color bucket, rounded to a whole percent. It is an estimate rather than an exact count because pixels are bucketed. Use it to judge which tones dominate the composition.
Can I use the values in CSS?::Yes. Each swatch is shown as HEX, RGB and HSL, and the CSS block wraps them in custom properties. Paste the block into a root rule and reference the variables anywhere in your styles. The HEX form is the shortest for hand edits.
Does the tool upload my image?::No. The file is decoded by the browser, drawn on a local canvas and read there. The swatches and copied strings are produced in this tab. Closing the page discards the image, and the sample button generates its own test strip locally.
Why does the palette change with size?::A smaller palette merges nearby shades into broader groups, while a larger one splits them into finer swatches. The sampling method stays the same, so the colors remain related. Try a few sizes to find the summary that suits your design.
Are the colors taken from my image?::Yes. The palette is calculated from the pixels of the uploaded file. Transparent pixels are skipped and similar shades are grouped, so the swatches describe what is visible in the picture. Changing the color count recalculates the palette from the same sampled pixels.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an Image Cropper?
page.whatIs:
Cropping removes pixels from the edges of an image so the subject fills the frame. Unlike resizing, which changes every pixel, cropping keeps the remaining pixels at their original sharpness. You choose a rectangle inside the source, and the browser draws only that region onto a new canvas. Nothing outside the box reaches the exported file, but the original file on your device is untouched.

An aspect preset fixes the shape of that rectangle. Free lets you choose width and height independently. Square, four by three, sixteen by nine and three by four keep a fixed width to height relationship, so social posts, banners and portrait thumbnails fit their target slots without stretching. Changing a preset recenters the box, and you can still drag it or edit the offset numbers to recompose the shot.

A circular crop clips the rectangle to a circle before export. The area outside the circle becomes transparent, which works with PNG and WebP. JPEG cannot store transparency, so those corners are filled with the page surface colour instead. The overlay on the preview uses the same rounded shape, so what you see matches the downloaded file.

Output format decides how the cropped pixels are encoded. PNG is lossless and preserves transparency, JPEG is compact for photographs, and WebP offers good quality at smaller sizes. Quality applies to JPEG and WebP only. The tool caps files at 20 MB and canvas sides at 8192 pixels, and the sample button draws a test image locally so you can try the flow.

Shapes are applied as an export mask. A rectangle keeps every pixel inside the frame. A square locks the frame to a one to one ratio, which suits profile pictures and product tiles. A circle clips the crop to a round avatar, and a rounded rectangle softens the corners for cards and thumbnails. The source image is never changed, only the exported copy.

The crop frame can be moved with a mouse, a trackpad or touch. Four corner handles resize the frame directly, while the numeric fields give exact pixel values when precision matters. Aspect presets clamp the frame to a chosen ratio, and the live preview shows how much of the original image will remain after export.

Six crop shapes are available: rectangle, square, circle, rounded rectangle, pill and triangle. Each shape is applied as an export mask, so you can try several from the same source image without uploading again. Every crop is encoded as PNG, JPEG and WebP at the same time, which gives you three download variations from one frame. The inline badge shows the crop dimensions and the estimated output size before you choose a file.

The crop frame is controlled by dragging its body or any of the four corner handles. Use the aspect pills for a fixed ratio, then open Precision and Export Settings when you need exact offset and size values. The result updates on every change, so the download buttons always match the frame you see.

page.guidanceTitle: Choosing a crop shape and export format

Start with the shape you need, not with the picture. A square suits profile avatars, sixteen by nine suits video thumbnails, and three by four suits portrait posts. Once a preset is active, the width and height stay linked, so edit one side and the other follows the ratio. Dragging the overlay moves the box without changing its size, which makes it easy to keep a face centered while you recompose.

Choose PNG when transparency matters, especially with a circular crop. Choose JPEG for photographs where a smaller file helps, and WebP when you want both compression and an alpha channel. Quality only changes lossy output. Very large dimensions take longer to encode, and canvas sizes above eight thousand pixels per side may fail on some devices, so keep the crop modest when you can.

page.whatIsTitle: What is Image to Base64?
page.whatIs:
A Data URL embeds a file directly inside a text string. Instead of pointing to a separate image file, the browser reads the encoded bytes from the URL itself. Base64 maps binary data to printable ASCII characters, so an image can travel inside CSS, HTML or JSON without a second request.

The prefix records the MIME type, which tells the browser how to interpret the bytes. This tool detects the type from the local file and writes data:image/png;base64 or the matching JPEG, WebP or GIF form. Keeping the MIME accurate matters because a wrong prefix can make the image fail to render.

The result pane offers three copy ready forms: the raw Data URL, a CSS background-image declaration and a complete HTML img element. Each can be pasted into a stylesheet or document. Large images produce very long strings, so a warning appears when the source exceeds about 1.5 MB.

Decoding works in reverse. Paste any image Data URL, and the tool splits the prefix from the payload, rebuilds the bytes locally and offers a preview plus a downloaded file. Nothing is uploaded, and the object URL used for the preview is released when you reset or leave the tool.

Base64 is a text encoding for binary data. A Data URL places that text in a single string that begins with a media type marker, so a browser can render the image without a separate file request. This is useful for small icons, inline previews and self contained HTML examples, but it makes the source about thirty three percent larger than the original bytes.

The two directions are kept separate on purpose. Image to Base reads a local file and produces the Data URL, a CSS background rule and an HTML img tag. Base to Image takes a pasted Data URL, decodes its bytes locally and offers a preview and download. Keeping the flows apart avoids mixing an upload field with a paste field in one confusing screen.

page.guidanceTitle: When to embed images as Data URLs
page.guidance:
Data URLs shine when an image is tiny and reused often, such as a one pixel tracker, a small icon or a background inside a single HTML file. They remove an extra request and keep everything self contained. They also work well in generated stylesheets where a separate asset folder would be awkward.

Base64 adds roughly a third to the byte count, and the string cannot be cached as a separate resource. For photographs or large artwork, prefer a normal image file and let the browser cache it. page.whatIsTitle: What is JSON to TypeScript?
page.whatIs:
TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, and an interface describes the shape an object is expected to have. Generating that shape from a sample JSON document saves typing and gives editors useful completion. Each value in the sample becomes a field with an inferred type.

Strings, numbers and booleans map directly. Nested objects become nested object types, and arrays become arrays of their element type. When an array contains objects, the tool writes a named interface for the common shape and a type alias for the list, so a repeated item is declared once.

Optional inference looks across every item in an array. A key that appears in only some items gets a question mark, which reflects real world API payloads where fields are sometimes absent. Nullable inference keeps null in the type when the sample contains it, instead of pretending the field is always a string or number.

Generated types are a starting point, not a contract. A single sample cannot reveal every value an API may return, so review the output before relying on it. The root name control avoids generic names in a shared codebase, and the result can be copied or downloaded as a ts file.

page.guidanceTitle: Turning a sample payload into dependable types
page.guidance:
Feed the tool a representative payload, not a single hand picked example. Arrays with several objects let optional inference see which keys truly vary. If every item has the same keys, no field becomes optional, which may be exactly right. A sample that includes null values will produce a wider type, and that wider type is usually safer than one that assumes perfection.

Keep the root name meaningful, such as User or OrderItem, because generated types often live in shared folders. The interface style suits object shapes that may be extended later, while a type alias suits unions and simple records. Treat the output as a draft to review, then tighten it once you know the full range of data your source can return.

Is the generated type complete?::No. It describes only the JSON you pasted, so a field that never appears in the sample cannot be predicted. Use a broad sample with several array items, then review the result. Generated types work best as a first draft that you refine against real responses.
What makes a field optional?::When the root is an array of objects, a key missing from any item is marked optional if optional fields are enabled. A key present in every item stays required. This mirrors common API payloads where some records carry extra detail and others do not.
How are arrays handled?::An array of objects produces a named interface for the shared shape and a type alias for the list. Arrays of primitives become arrays of the inferred scalar type. An empty array becomes an array of unknown until you provide a sample with an element.
What does nullable do?::With nullable types enabled, a null value produces a union such as string or null. With it disabled, null values are skipped when the field type is inferred. Keeping null is usually more honest for API data because missing and empty values are different states.
Is my JSON sent anywhere?::No. Parsing and generation run in this tab with the browser JSON engine. Nothing is uploaded or stored. Closing the page clears the input, and the download is assembled locally from the generated text as a blob.
Can I use a type alias instead?::Yes. The style control switches the root declaration between an interface and a type alias. Nested object shapes stay inline, and array items still get a named interface so the output remains readable. Copy or download either form.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Line Prefix Suffix tool?
page.whatIs:
A line prefix suffix tool applies the same edit to every row of a text block. You provide a list, then choose text to place before each line, text to place after it, and an optional wrapper that surrounds the line itself. Numbering can be switched on, and blank rows can be dropped or kept. The preview shows the exact result.

The work is string based rather than regex based. The input is split on line breaks, each remaining row is assembled from the chosen parts, and the rows are joined again. Because the order is fixed, you can combine a bullet prefix with a closing suffix and a quote wrapper without writing a formula. A starting number sets the first value, and later rows count upward from there.

Blank line handling changes the character of the result. Skipping empty rows produces a compact list with consecutive numbers, which suits a cleaned export. Keeping them preserves the layout of a template, a code block or a form where an empty row still has meaning. Both modes are useful, so the choice stays with you.

Everything runs in the browser. No line is uploaded and there is no account. The numbering and blank line settings are remembered on this device, while the text and affixes you type are cleared on refresh, which keeps the workspace predictable between visits.

Numbering works best on short, stable lists where the order will not change after you paste. Add more than one decoration only when each one has a clear purpose.

Blank lines deserve a moment of attention. Keeping only non-empty lines produces a compact result with consecutive numbers, which suits a cleaned list. Keeping all lines preserves the original spacing and is better for templates or code blocks where an empty row still carries meaning. page.whatIsTitle: What is a password strength checker?
page.whatIs:
A password strength checker is a local evaluator that looks at a phrase and estimates how difficult it would be to guess. It does not crack the password and it does not know the rules of the service where you will use it. Instead, it measures visible signals such as total length, which character sets appear and whether the text follows a predictable shape.

Length is the strongest simple signal. A phrase of sixteen characters drawn from letters, digits and symbols has a far larger search space than a short word with one symbol added. Entropy is a way of expressing that space in bits: a higher number means an attacker would need more guesses on average. This tool estimates entropy from the character groups actually present and subtracts value when it sees an obvious sequence or repeated block.

Pattern checks catch phrases that look long but are easy to guess. A run of adjacent letters, a repeated two character block, a familiar word or a standard number string all reduce real strength. The report lists each check as passed or failed, so you can see why a score moved rather than trusting a single colour. Tips point at the specific change with the biggest payoff.

The score is a guide rather than a promise. A determined attacker with a stolen hash and powerful hardware can still guess a phrase that scores well, and a service may impose its own character rules. The important practical point is privacy: this workspace runs entirely in your browser tab, so the password you type is never stored, uploaded or shared.

Edit the phrase and repeat until the report looks acceptable.
page.guidanceTitle: Why length and patterns matter
page.guidance:
Start with length rather than decoration. Adding characters multiplies the search space, while appending a single symbol to a short word adds very little. A passphrase made from several unusual words can be easier to remember and harder to guess than a compact string of random looking substitutions. The minimum length field lets you test your own target, so a phrase can be judged against the policy of the service you plan to use.

Patterns are what make a long phrase weak. Adjacent runs such as abcd, repeated blocks and familiar words are the first things a guessing tool tries, so the checker subtracts for them and shows a failed check. Use the tips to replace one weak element at a time and watch how the estimate responds. Treat the result as a quick local signal, not a security audit: a unique phrase per account and a password manager still do most of the work. Nothing you type is transmitted or retained after you close the tab.

page.faqs:
Is my password sent anywhere?::No. Scoring happens in your browser tab using the text you type. There is no request to a server, no account and no saved history. Closing the page removes the value from memory, and the clear action empties the field immediately if you want to test another phrase.
How is the entropy estimate calculated?::The tool looks at which character groups appear, such as lowercase, uppercase, digits and symbols, then multiplies the pool size by the length in a logarithmic calculation. It subtracts a penalty when it finds a sequence, a repeated block or a familiar word. The number is a useful comparison, not a guarantee.
Why does a long phrase still score weakly?::Length alone does not help if the text is predictable. A repeated character, an alphabetical run or a common word gives a guessing tool an easy starting point. The failed check list names the exact pattern, and the tips suggest how to replace it while keeping the phrase memorable.
Should I use symbols instead of more characters?::Usually length wins. A longer phrase drawn from a broad set creates more possible combinations than a short phrase with a couple of symbols swapped in. Use symbols as one part of a varied mixture, and prefer a phrase you can recall without writing down.
Does this replace a password manager?::No. A manager generates unique random phrases for every account and stores them safely. This checker is a quick way to compare candidates before you save one. Unique credentials per site matter more than any single score, so avoid reusing a phrase even when it rates highly here.
What does the minimum length field change?::It sets the target used by the length check, from four to thirty two characters. Lowering or raising it updates the report instantly without changing the phrase itself. Choose a value that reflects the policy of the service, then use the remaining checks to judge overall quality.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a PPI calculator?
page.whatIs:
PPI stands for pixels per inch. It describes how densely pixels are packed along a physical distance, which is what makes an image look sharp or soft on a screen or in print. A calculator takes the pixel width and height and combines them with a diagonal measurement to produce that density figure.

This tool squares the pixel dimensions, takes the square root through the pixel diagonal, and divides by the diagonal in inches. The result is rounded to one decimal place for display. It also reports megapixels, which is the pixel count divided by one million, and a reduced aspect ratio that expresses the shape with small whole numbers.

A preview rectangle scales the proportions to fit the result pane. It is not a picture of your content, only a shape guide that makes an unusually wide or tall format easy to spot. Copy and download actions package the numbers together when you need to share them with a colleague or paste them into a spec.

Every value is computed locally. Nothing is uploaded or stored, and the sample button fills a common 1920 by 1080 example across 24 inches so you can check the maths at once. For the underlying idea, see the trusted reference linked in the About this tool section.

What does PPI actually measure?::PPI measures how many pixels occupy one inch of physical space. A higher number usually means finer detail when the image is viewed at a normal distance. It depends on both the pixel dimensions and the size at which those pixels are shown, so the same image can have different densities on two displays.
Which diagonal should I enter?::Use the measured diagonal of the screen or printed area you care about, expressed in inches. For a monitor, that is the advertised panel size. For a print, measure corner to corner across the finished area. The file itself has no physical size until you choose how large to display or print it.
How is the result calculated?::The tool finds the pixel diagonal with the square root of width squared plus height squared, then divides that value by the diagonal in inches. Megapixels come from width times height divided by one million, and the aspect ratio is reduced by the greatest common factor of the two pixel dimensions.
Why does the preview rectangle look small?::The preview is scaled to fit the stage while preserving the exact proportions of your dimensions. It is a shape guide rather than a full size picture. A very wide or tall input will therefore appear as a long thin or short wide rectangle, which is often exactly what you need to notice before cropping.
What if a field is empty or zero?::The tool waits until all three fields have values. If a number is missing, text was entered, or a value is zero or negative, it shows a short error and a fix hint beside the fields. Enter positive numbers and the density, megapixels and shape appear again immediately.
Is the calculation private?::Yes. Width, height and diagonal are processed entirely in this tab. There is no network request and no saved record of your inputs. You can copy or download the summary if you need it elsewhere, and resetting the tool clears every field from the interface.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a robots.txt generator?
page.whatIs:
robots.txt is a plain text file placed at the root of a site. It gives crawlers instructions about which paths they may request. A typical rule names a user agent, then lists allow and disallow paths. Crawlers read the file before fetching pages, so it works as a request rather than an enforcement mechanism.

The file is a set of groups separated by blank lines. Each group starts with one or more User-agent lines, followed by the paths that apply to that agent. A star matches every crawler. Specific agents such as Googlebot can get their own group with different rules.

Crawl-delay asks a crawler to wait between requests. Some search engines honour it and others ignore it, so it is a polite suggestion rather than a guarantee. A Sitemap line points crawlers to an XML index of your pages, which helps discovery even when links are hard to follow.

This generator keeps the syntax tidy and checks the parts that are easy to get wrong. Paths must begin with a slash, the delay must be a whole number and the sitemap must be an absolute http or https URL. The preview shows exactly what will be saved.

page.guidanceTitle: Writing crawler rules that stay easy to maintain
page.guidance:
Order groups from specific to general. Crawlers choose the most specific matching user agent, so a Googlebot group should come before a star group that applies to everyone else. Keep paths rooted at the site root and put one path on each line. A trailing slash covers a directory and everything below it, which is simpler than listing each subpage.

Use the sample as a starting point and then trim it to your site. A disallow line hides a path from many crawlers but does not remove it from search results if other pages link to it. For sensitive areas use authentication instead. Check the generated text after every edit so the preview matches what you will publish at your domain root. Review it again before a site launch.

Where does robots.txt have to live?::It must be served at the root of the domain, for example example.com/robots.txt. A file in a subfolder is not read for the whole site. Download the generated file and place it there, then request the URL in a browser to confirm it is public.
Does disallow remove a page from search?::No. A disallow line asks compliant crawlers not to fetch a path, but existing results can remain until the crawler revisits and sees the change. For a page that must disappear, remove links to it and use a noindex meta tag or a suitable HTTP header instead.
What does the star user agent mean?::A star means the rules apply to every crawler that does not have a more specific group. Treat it as a polite request that can reduce load for bots that support it, not as a hard rate control. If a server needs strict protection, use server side throttling or access rules instead.
Can I list more than one path?::Yes. Put each path on its own line in the allow or disallow box. The generator prints one directive per line in the same order. Paths must start with a slash, and the inline error tells you which group needs correcting if a line is missing it.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an ROI Calculator?
page.whatIs:
Return on investment, usually shortened to ROI, measures the gain from a project against the money put into it. The basic calculation divides net profit by the initial investment and multiplies by one hundred. A result of 45 percent means the project returned forty five units of profit for every hundred units committed. A negative result describes a loss.

This tool also reports the ending value and the money multiple. Ending value is the original investment plus net profit, while the multiple divides that ending value by the amount invested. A multiple of 1.45 means each unit invested grew to one point four five units, including the original capital. The two figures help when ROI alone feels abstract.

The annualised figure converts total return into a yearly rate. It assumes the investment grew by the same compound rate each year across the period you enter. A short project and a long project can share the same total ROI while producing very different yearly results, so the annualised rate supports a fairer comparison. When the ending value is negative, no real compound rate exists and the tool leaves that field blank.

All arithmetic happens in the browser. The calculator does not track individual cash flows or fees, so enter the profit figure after every cost you want included. Nothing is uploaded and no account is needed.

page.guidanceTitle: Interpreting ROI and Annual Return
page.guidance:
Return on investment is a simple ratio: net profit divided by the amount put in. A result of 45 percent means every hundred units invested returned forty five units of profit. The money multiple adds the original capital back, so the same example ends at one point four five times the starting amount. Read the three figures together, because each answers a different question about the same project.

Annualised return puts projects of different lengths on a common footing. Two years and ten years can produce the same total ROI while delivering very different yearly results, so the compound annual growth rate is often the fairer comparison. Enter the full holding period in years, including fractions where useful. A negative ending value has no meaningful compound rate, and the result pane says so plainly rather than showing a misleading figure.

page.faqs:
What exactly does ROI measure?::Return on investment divides net profit by the original outlay and multiplies by one hundred. It answers how much gain was produced for each unit of capital committed. A negative profit gives a negative percentage, which shows a loss. The tool keeps the input in ordinary currency units, so the ratio works with dollars, euros or any other consistent unit.
What is the money multiple?::The money multiple is the ending value divided by the starting investment. A multiple of 1.45 means you finish with one point four five units for every unit you began with, including the original capital. It is useful beside ROI because it shows the total returned amount rather than only the gain.
How is the annualised rate found?::The annualised figure treats the ending value as the result of steady yearly compounding over the period you enter. It takes the ratio of ending to starting value, raises it to the power of one divided by the years, and subtracts one. The result is shown as a percentage next to the total ROI for comparison.
Can I use a loss as the profit value?::Yes. A negative profit represents money lost on the project, and the tool subtracts it from the investment to find the ending value. ROI becomes negative and the money multiple falls below one. If the loss is larger than the investment, the ending value is negative and no compound annual rate is reported.
Does the tool account for extra costs?::Use the net profit field for the figure after every cost, fee and tax you want included. The calculator does not track individual expense rows, so adding those entries before you type the profit keeps the ratio honest. Cash flows spread over several years are treated as one total, not as separate deposits.
Are my figures stored or uploaded?::No. All arithmetic happens inside this page and the clipboard is the only way the summary leaves it. There is no upload, no account and no analytics event tied to your numbers. Refreshing clears the three fields, so the tool is safe to use with sensitive financial plans.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Roman numeral converter?
page.whatIs:
A Roman numeral converter translates between the decimal numbers used every day and the letter based system of ancient Rome. Roman notation uses the symbols I, V, X, L, C, D and M, and places a smaller symbol before a larger one to subtract a value. The form IV means four, while VI means six.

This tool works in both directions from a single field. A number is read as a decimal value and written in canonical subtractive form. Roman letters are read back into a number, then checked by rebuilding the canonical form. If the two strings do not match, the tool reports an error instead of showing a value that would be rejected elsewhere.

The supported range runs from 1 to 3999, which covers classical notation without overlines or special symbols for larger values. Uppercase and lowercase letters are both accepted, and surrounding spaces are ignored. Sixteen quick examples highlight the subtractive pairs and a familiar year so you can confirm the behaviour at a glance.

Conversion is entirely local. Nothing is sent to a server, and the result can be copied with a button or a keyboard shortcut. For background on the notation itself, see the trusted reference linked in the About this tool section below.

Keep the value between one and 3999, because classical Roman notation has no standard symbol above three thousand. Use subtractive forms such as IV, IX, XL and CM rather than additive runs like VIIII. The tool checks the order of every symbol and shows an error with a fix hint if the form is not canonical. Quick example buttons cover the subtractive pairs and a larger year, which makes it easy to verify the result before you copy it.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an SVG optimizer?
page.whatIs:
An SVG optimizer rewrites vector markup so the same picture takes fewer bytes. It keeps the shapes, paths and styles intact while removing text that browsers never render, such as comments and editor notes. The result is still plain SVG that any browser or design tool can open.

The cleanup is deliberately conservative. Comments are dropped, metadata and desc blocks are removed, and editor namespaces such as inkscape and sodipodi are stripped from tags. Whitespace outside quoted values is collapsed, so path data and colour values keep their exact characters.

The JSX option renames attributes for React style components. Kebab case names become camel case, class becomes className and for becomes htmlFor. Quoted values are left alone, which matters for path strings and data URLs. The option only changes attribute names, never geometry.

Before writing output, the tool checks that the input starts with an svg root and that every tag closes in order. Errors name the problem and suggest a fix rather than guessing. Byte counts before and after show how much was saved, and the result can be copied or downloaded.

The optimizer keeps the SVG element tree intact and removes only redundant material. Comments, editor metadata and repeated whitespace are safe to drop. Optional JSX conversion changes hyphenated attribute names into camelCase for React projects while leaving the geometry untouched.

A side by side layout makes review quick. The source stays on the left and the cleaned markup on the right, with byte counts and a saved percentage above the output. Paste markup from a design export, compare the two blocks, then copy or download the result when it looks right.

page.guidanceTitle: Choosing cleanup options for production SVG files
page.guidance:
Start with comment and metadata removal for assets exported from a vector editor. Those two options usually produce the largest saving because editor previews and notes can outweigh the drawing itself. Keep whitespace collapse enabled for web delivery, since compact markup parses quickly and stays readable enough for review. Disable it only when you need the original line structure for a documentation example.

The JSX switch is for component work, not for files served as images. It renames stroke-width to strokeWidth and class to className while protecting quoted path data. If the SVG still has an xmlns attribute, keep it when the file is used standalone and remove it when a framework supplies the namespace. Check the byte counter after each change so the saving is visible before you copy.

Does optimization change the picture?::No. The cleanup removes comments, editor metadata and redundant whitespace while keeping shapes, path data and colours unchanged. The browser paints the same geometry from a smaller string. If you enable JSX attributes, only attribute names change, never coordinates or styles.
Why is my SVG rejected?::The tool requires a document with an svg root element and tags that open and close in the right order. It also rejects files over 200,000 characters. The inline message names the problem and suggests the fix, so you can correct the source and paste it again.
What does metadata removal delete?::It removes metadata, title and desc elements and attributes from common vector editors such as inkscape and sodipodi. Those entries are useful while designing but rarely needed in a published asset. Turn the option off if credits or accessibility descriptions must stay in the file.
Will quoted path data stay intact?::Yes. Whitespace collapse and attribute renaming only work outside quoted values. A path string keeps its spaces, commas and letters exactly as written, and a data URL is never rewritten. This is why tokenising the markup is safer than a plain find and replace.
When should I use JSX attributes?::Use that option when the output goes into a React or JSX file. It changes names such as stroke-width to strokeWidth and class to className, which are required by JSX. Leave it off for SVG files served directly from a server or opened in a design tool.
Is my SVG uploaded anywhere?::No. All tokenising, cleanup and counting happen in your browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server, and the pasted markup is not written to storage. Only the four option choices are remembered on this device so the same settings are ready on your next visit.
Does optimization change the drawing?::No. The tool removes comments, metadata and repeated whitespace, and it can rename attributes for JSX. Paths, shapes, fills and viewBox values stay as they are. Compare the source and result side by side, then copy the version you want to use.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Timezone Converter?
page.whatIs:
A time zone converter translates one wall-clock time into the equivalent local time elsewhere. You supply a date, a time and the zone that clock belongs to. The tool turns that wall time into a single instant, then formats the same instant in each selected target zone. The result includes the weekday, date, local clock and the offset against the base.

The conversion uses named zones from the IANA time zone database rather than fixed offsets. That matters because many regions change their offset for daylight saving. A zone that is five hours behind in January might be four hours behind in July, so a fixed guess would produce the wrong hour for part of the year. The correct rules come from the browser's internationalisation support.

An hour adjustment field shifts the moment before conversion without changing the selected zones. Use it to test a meeting moved by a few hours or to compare a deadline at another point in the day. Negative values move the moment earlier and positive values move it later. The quick buttons cover common shifts, while the number field accepts finer changes.

Everything happens in the page. No date, time or zone list is uploaded, and only your zone choices and adjustment are remembered on this device. Copy the finished list when you are ready to share it.

page.guidanceTitle: Planning Across Multiple Time Zones
page.guidance:
A converted time is only as good as the base you give it. Choose the zone where the original wall time was written, not the zone of the person reading the result. Check the date as well as the clock, because a late evening appointment can land on the following day in another region. The list keeps both fields together so an invite does not go out with the right hour and the wrong date.

Daylight saving shifts mean a fixed offset is not safe across a whole year. This tool uses the IANA time zone database through the browser, so the same input produces the correct local clock in summer and winter. Use the hour controls when you want to test a scenario rather than a real zone. Select only the regions you need, and copy the summary once the list looks right.

What does the base zone mean?::The base zone tells the tool which local clock your entered date and time belong to. If an invitation says 09:30 in London, choose London as the base before converting it. Choosing UTC instead would treat the same digits as a UTC clock and shift every result by the London offset for that day.
How do the hour controls work?::The hour field and quick buttons shift the chosen moment before it is converted, without changing which zones are selected. Use a negative value to move earlier or a positive value to move later. This is handy for testing a meeting moved by a few hours or for checking what a deadline looks like at another point in the day.
Does it handle daylight saving?::Yes. Conversion uses the named zone rather than a fixed offset, so the browser applies the daylight saving rule in force on your chosen date. A London meeting in July and the same meeting in January can differ by an hour against New York. Always pick a real date instead of relying on a remembered offset.
Why is a target on a different day?::Time zones can be many hours apart, so a morning meeting in one region may be late evening or tomorrow in another. page.whatIsTitle: What is a Unicode inspector?
page.whatIs:
A Unicode inspector reads text code point by code point and reports characters that do not print visibly. Common examples include the zero width space used to join or split words, the non breaking space that prevents a line break, and direction marks that change how mixed scripts are displayed. Each one is valid Unicode but can be surprising when it is copied between apps.

This tool walks the pasted string and groups flagged characters into four families: zero width, non breaking, directional and control. It shows the position, the hexadecimal code and a readable name for every match. Ordinary letters, digits and punctuation are counted but not listed, so the table stays focused on the characters you cannot see.

Cleaning is controlled by four switches. Zero width, direction and control characters are deleted, while non breaking spaces are replaced with an ordinary space so words remain separate. The cleaned text appears in its own field and can be copied in one click. Changing a switch updates the result immediately.

All inspection happens inside this tab. Your text is not uploaded, indexed or stored, which makes the tool suitable for drafts and private messages. For details about the invisible characters themselves, see the trusted reference linked in the About this tool section below.

page.guidanceTitle: How to clean invisible formatting
page.guidance:
Paste a suspicious string into the input pane and read the flagged count first. Zero width characters can join words that should be separate, while non breaking spaces prevent a natural line break in a heading. Direction marks can reverse the order of letters in a mixed language sentence. The table shows the exact code point and position so you can decide what to keep.

Enable only the categories you want to remove. Zero width, direction and control characters are deleted, while non breaking spaces become ordinary spaces so words stay readable. Copy the cleaned text when it looks right, then paste it back into your document. Recheck the result, because a second hidden character may have been revealed once the first one was removed.

page.faqs:
Which characters does the tool detect?::It checks for zero width characters such as the zero width space and word joiner, non breaking spaces such as the figure space, direction marks such as the right to left mark, and control characters. Ordinary letters, numbers and punctuation are counted but are not listed in the table.
Why replace a non breaking space instead of deleting it?::Deleting it would push two words together and change the meaning of the text. Replacing it with an ordinary space keeps the word boundary while allowing a normal line break. Zero width and direction characters are removed because they carry no visible content of their own.
What does the position column mean?::It is the one based index of the character in your pasted string, counting each Unicode code point once. Emoji made from several code points may occupy more than one position. The hexadecimal code column is the reliable identifier when you compare the result with a specification or a debugging log.
Can I keep a category in the cleaned text?::Yes. Each group has its own switch. Turn a switch off and characters from that group are left exactly as they were in the source. The cleaned text, its length and the table update as soon as you change a switch, so you can compare different choices quickly.
Does the tool change visible characters?::No. Only characters in the four inspectable groups are touched, and only when their switch is on. Letters, digits, emoji and punctuation pass through unchanged. Non breaking spaces become ordinary spaces, which is the one intentional substitution and is described beside the switches.
Is my text uploaded or saved?::No. Inspection and cleaning both run in this tab using local code. There is no network request and no stored copy of what you paste. The cleaned text stays on screen until you copy it or replace the input, and resetting the tool clears the text and restores the default switches.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a URL parser?
page.whatIs:
A URL parser takes one address and separates it into the pieces that a browser uses to find a resource. The scheme, such as https, tells the client which protocol to speak. The host names the server, an optional port selects a service, and the path identifies the resource on that server. A fragment after the hash points to a position inside the document and is never sent in the request.

The query string holds named parameters. Each pair has a key and a value, separated by an equals sign, and pairs are joined with an ampersand. Values are percent encoded so spaces, slashes and non ASCII characters travel safely. A parser decodes those values for display, shows one editable row per pair, and encodes them again when the link is rebuilt. Repeated keys remain separate rows in their original order.

This workspace uses the URL object built into the platform, so parsing follows the same rules that browsers apply. A full address needs a scheme and usually a host. A string such as /products?page=2 is a relative reference and cannot be parsed on its own because the browser has no base to resolve it against. The tool explains that case with a fix hint instead of returning a broken result.

Editing the parts is useful when a link has grown hard to read or a tracking value needs to change. The rebuilt output is shown as plain text with copy and download actions, and the host and parameter count are summarised beside it. No address is stored, logged or sent to another server, so you can inspect private staging links without sharing them.

page.guidanceTitle: How to read and rebuild a URL
page.guidance:
Treat the query string as data rather than as part of the address structure. A key such as page or category has a meaning defined by the site that receives it, so changing a name changes the request even when the host stays the same. Because each pair is encoded independently, a value can safely contain spaces, slashes and punctuation. The decoded rows you see here are a viewing convenience; the rebuilt link always encodes them again.

When you share a rebuilt address, check the fragment as well as the query. A fragment after the hash directs a browser to a section of the page but is not sent to the server, so it can survive a change of host while the rest of the address points somewhere new. If an address contains sensitive tokens in its parameters, treat the copied link like a password and avoid pasting it into public places. The tool keeps everything in this tab and clears the result when you start again.

Path: /products
Fragment: reviews
Query: category=tools, page=2
Rebuilt: http://example.com/products?category=tools&page=2#reviews

What counts as a full URL?::A full URL has a scheme such as https followed by a host such as example.com. A path on its own is a relative reference, and the tool cannot resolve it without a base address. Paste the complete link and every part will appear in the edit pane.
Why are my query values decoded?::The query string stores encoded text so spaces and symbols survive transport. The parser decodes each value for display, which makes editing easier. When you copy the rebuilt link, those values are encoded once more, so the result remains a valid address.
Can I have two parameters with the same name?::Yes. Each pair is its own row, so repeated names stay in order and are rebuilt as separate pairs. That matters for APIs which read repeated keys as a list. Removing one row leaves the others untouched, and adding a new row does not disturb the existing values.
Does the fragment get sent to the server?::No. Text after the hash is used by the browser to find a position in the page and is left out of the network request. It still appears in the rebuilt link, so you can keep or change it. This makes it easy to point a shared address at a particular section while editing the query.
Where does my URL go after I paste it?::Nowhere. Parsing and rebuilding happen in your browser tab with the platform URL API. There is no request to a server and no history of pasted addresses. Closing the tab clears the work, and the reset action returns the pane to the sample link.
What if I need a custom delimiter in a query?::Query pairs are joined with an ampersand by convention. A value that contains an ampersand must be encoded, and the tool handles that when it rebuilds the link. If a service uses a different convention, edit the resulting text directly rather than changing the row values.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an XML to JSON converter?
page.whatIs:
An XML to JSON converter reads an XML document and expresses the same information as a JSON object. XML stores data in nested elements with named attributes, while JSON uses keys, strings, arrays and objects. A conversion maps one structure to the other so the data can be used by APIs, configuration files and modern application code.

This tool parses your document with the browser XML parser, then walks the resulting tree locally. Attributes become keys with an @ prefix when you keep them in prefixed mode. Repeated element names are grouped into arrays, so a list of records stays a list even when it contains a single item. Element text is trimmed by default and placed under a text key when the element also has attributes.

You can switch attributes off when you only need values, and turn whitespace trimming off when spaces at the edges of a value matter. The output is formatted with either two or four spaces per level. Choose the style that matches the file you are pasting into, then copy the text or download it as a JSON file.

Because the whole conversion happens inside the tab, sensitive documents never leave your device. Validation is immediate: malformed XML produces a short error with a fix hint instead of a partial result. For background on the browser XML parser, see the trusted reference linked in the About this tool section below.

page.guidanceTitle: How to shape a useful JSON result
page.guidance:
Start with a small, well formed XML fragment so you can see how the converter treats attributes and repeated names. When attributes matter, keep the prefixed mode so keys such as @id stay visible beside the element text. When you only need the values, switch to ignore mode and the JSON becomes shorter and easier to map into an application model.

Repeated elements always become arrays, even when only one appears in your source. That keeps the shape stable when a feed later adds a second record. Turn off whitespace trimming only when leading spaces carry meaning, such as inside a code sample. Choose two space indentation for pasting into documentation and four spaces for a config file that follows a team style. Check the result pane before copying, then download the JSON if you need a clean file.
page.exampleLabel: A small library feed with two books
page.exampleInput:
<library>
  <book id="b1">
    <title>Private XML</title>
  </book>
  <book id="b2">
    <title>Browser Tools</title>
  </book>
</library>
page.exampleNote: The two book elements become one array, and each id attribute becomes a key beginning with @.
page.features:
Attribute handling::Keep attributes as prefixed keys or ignore them for a leaner object.
Repeated elements::Group sibling elements with the same name into arrays automatically.
Whitespace control::Trim surrounding text by default with an option to preserve it.
Indentation choice::Format the output with two or four spaces per level.
Instant validation::Show an error and a clear fix hint when the XML is malformed.
Private conversion::Parse and format the document inside the browser tab only.
page.useCases:
API prototyping::Turn a sample XML response into JSON for a mock endpoint.
Config migration::Move legacy XML settings into a JSON based application.
Data inspection::Read a small feed as a structured object before writing code.
Documentation::Paste readable JSON into a guide with your preferred indentation.
page.faqs:
Where do attributes go?::In prefixed mode each attribute becomes a key starting with @ inside its element object. This keeps attribute values separate from child elements and from the element text. Switch to ignore mode when those values are not needed and you want a smaller object that is easier to read.
Why is one record wrapped in an array?::Repeated element names always become arrays so that the JSON shape does not change when another record appears. A single book is stored the same way as ten books. That consistency makes it much simpler to write code that reads the result without checking whether the value is an object or a list.
How is element text stored?::An element that only contains text becomes a plain string. When the same element also has attributes or child elements, its text is placed under a dedicated text key so it does not collide with the other keys. Surrounding whitespace is removed by default to keep values clean.
What if my XML has an error?::The browser parser reports the first problem it finds and the tool shows a short error with a fix hint. Check for unclosed tags, mismatched tag names and unquoted attribute values. Correct the source text and the JSON result appears again immediately without reloading the page.
Does the tool support huge documents?::It handles typical configuration files and feed samples well. Very large documents can make any browser parser slow, so split them into smaller pieces when the page becomes sluggish. The tool stays entirely local, so splitting the source does not expose any of your data.
Is my XML uploaded anywhere?::No. Parsing and formatting both happen inside this tab with browser APIs. There is no network request, no analytics event and no stored copy of your document. The output can be copied or downloaded, and clearing the input removes it from the editor.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika converter desk. Parsing uses the standard browser XML parser and every document stays on your device. Reviewed 28 November 2026. Technical details are documented at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DOMParser.

about.title: About Toolpika
about.description: Toolpika is a collection of small utilities that run in your browser.
about.intro: Toolpika is a collection of small utilities. Each does one job, without asking you to sign up.
about.privacyBody: Every tool that touches a file or text processes it inside your browser. Nothing is uploaded, so we never see your content.
about.contactBody: Mail us and a human replies.
about.perkInstantBody: Every tool opens in a tab and works the moment you load it.
about.perkSmallBody: One job per tool, so there is nothing to learn before you begin.
about.believeTitle: Useful tools should stay out of the way.
about.believeBody: No accounts, no uploads and no clutter. Just a quiet collection of utilities that do one job well and leave when you are done.
about.storyTitle: Built for the small jobs, every day.
about.storyBody1: Toolpika started as a set of private utilities for everyday work. Each one solved a single annoyance without asking for a sign-up or sending a file to a server.
about.storyBody2: That idea still drives the site. Tools stay local, pages stay light and the collection grows only when something is genuinely useful.
about.specificBody: Tell us what you need and we will look at it. We read every request.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.description: What Toolpika does with your data. Which is very little.
privacy.filesBody: Tools that accept files run entirely in your browser using the File and Canvas APIs. File contents are never sent to a server and are never stored.
privacy.dataBody: We do not require an account. We store your theme and language preference in your browser's local storage, which never leaves your device.
privacy.cookiesBody: Toolpika does not set tracking cookies. A single essential cookie may be used to remember your language preference.
privacy.dataList1: Theme and language preferences stay in your browser.
privacy.dataList2: No account is required to use any public tool.
privacy.dataList3: Request submissions are only stored when you choose to send one.
